The position of His saying "mulli'at harasan shadidan" is accusative, as the second object of "wajadna," since it is transitive to two objects; it is also permissible that it be transitive to one object, in which case the clause's position is accusative as a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, and "harasan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Its description with the singular is considered in terms of the wording, as one says "al-salaf al-salih," i.e., the righteous predecessors.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 72, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen﴾: that is, we, the company of the jinn, before this used to sit in the heavens on seats to listen, meaning places in which we sat to eavesdrop on news from the heavens. "Li-l-sam'" means seats existing for listening. "Maqā'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a noun of place. The rebellious jinn used to do this in order to hear news of the heavens from the angels and then convey it to the soothsayers (kahana). So God, exalted is He, guarded it by sending His Messenger (ﷺ) with flaming shooting stars. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿But whoever now listens will find a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾, that is, one is posted for him to be struck with it, or it is posted because of him to prevent him from listening. His words "al-'āna" (now) is a adverb of the present, and it is used figuratively for the future. The accusative of "rasadan" (lying in wait) is either as an attribute of "shihāban" (flame) or as an object of purpose. It is singular, but it may also be a collective noun like "al-haras" (the guard).

They have disagreed over whether the devils were struck with flames before the mission (al-mab'ath) or not. A group said: that did not happen.

Al-Wahidi related from Ma'mar, who said: I said to al-Zuhri: Were the stars thrown in the Jahiliyya? He said: Yes. I said: What do you think of His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in it﴾ and so on? He said: Its matter was made severe and intensified when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent.

Ibn Qutayba said: Stoning had occurred before his mission, but it was not like it in its severity of guarding after his mission. They used to steal some news in certain circumstances, but when he was sent they were prevented from that entirely.

'Abd al-Malik ibn Sabur said: The heavens were not guarded during the fatra (the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad). When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the heavens were guarded, the devils were struck with flames, and they were prevented from approaching the heaven.

Nafi' ibn Jubayr said: During the fatra, the devils used to listen and were not struck. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were struck with flames. The discussion of this has already preceded.

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾: that is, we do not know whether evil is intended for the people of the earth because of this guarding of the heaven, or whether their Lord intends for them rashad (guidance), that is, good.

Ibn Zayd said: Iblis said: We do not know whether God intended by this prevention to send down a punishment upon the people of the earth, or to send to them a messenger.

The word "sharrun" (evil) is in the nominative either by the construction of "ishtighāl" (the verb being occupied with the object, i.e., a verb governing a pronoun) or as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is what follows. The first is more preferable. The clause fills the place of the two objects of "nadri" (we know). The more appropriate view is that this is the speech of the jinn among themselves, not the speech of Iblis as Ibn Zayd said.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: that is, some said to others, when they called their companions to faith in Muhammad (ﷺ): We, before hearing the Qur'an, were among those described as righteous. ﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, a people below that, meaning below those described as righteous. It has been said that by "the righteous" he meant the believers, and by "those below that" the disbelievers. The first is more preferable.

The meaning of ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾ is: groups scattered apart and varied kinds. "Qidad" is the plural of "qidda," which is a piece of a thing. A people became "qidad" when their conditions became dispersed. From this is the poet's saying:

The one who holds back and extends, guiding to His obedience,
Amid the trials of people when their desires are scattered (qidad).

The meaning is: we were people of divergent paths, or our paths were divergent, or we were like divergent paths. From this is Labid's saying:

The eye did not reach all its desire
On the day the horses walk in scattered ranks (bi-l-qidad).

And his saying also:

And I said, while Zayd was bare-headed,
On the day the horses of 'Amr turned in scattered flight (qidadan).

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: they were different religions. Qatada said: they were divergent desires.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: They were Muslims, Jews, Christians, and Magians. Mujahid said the same.

Al-Hasan said: The jinn are like you, Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on faith), Rafida (those who reject the early caliphs), and Shi'a (partisans). Al-Suddi said the same.

﴿And that we thought that we would never escape God in the earth﴾: here "zanan" (thought) means knowledge and certainty. That is: we knew that the matter is that we will never escape God in the earth, wherever we are in it, nor will we outrun Him if He intends a matter for us. ﴿And we will never escape Him by fleeing﴾: that is, fleeing from it; so it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿we believed in it﴾, and we affirmed that it is from God, and we did not deny it as the disbelieving humans denied it. ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither loss (bakhsan) nor oppression (rahaqan)﴾: that is, he will not fear a deficiency in his deed and its reward, nor injustice and something hateful that covers him. "Bakhs" is deficiency, and "rahaq" is transgression and insolence. The meaning is: he will not fear that any of his good deeds will be diminished or that his evil deeds will be increased. The explanation of "rahaq" has already been given shortly before.

The majority recited "bakhsan" with a sukun on the kha'. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it with a fatha on it. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash recited "fa-lā yakhaf" (with a jussive) as an answer to the conditional, but there is no basis for this after the entry of the fa'. The implied meaning is: "fa-huwa lā yakhāf" (so he does not fear), and the matter is clear.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out with a group of his companions, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and the devils had been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars were sent against them. The devils returned to their people, and they said: What is wrong with you? They said: We have been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars have been sent against us. They said: Nothing has come between you and the news of the heaven except something that has happened. So strike the eastern and western parts of the earth, so that you may know what this matter is that has come between you and the news of the heaven. Those who had headed toward Tihama returned to the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was at Nakhla, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and he was leading his companions in the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an, they listened to it and said: By God, this is what has come between you and the news of the heaven. At that moment, when they returned to their people, they said: O our people, ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, ﴿It guides to righteousness, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. Then God revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾." What was revealed to him was the speech of the jinn.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾, that he said: They were from the jinn of Nasibin.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord﴾, that he said: His blessings and His greatness.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: His command and His power.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated (al-Suyuti said with a weak chain) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), concerning His words: ﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say﴾, that he said: It is Iblis.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa', al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ikrima ibn Abi al-Sa'ib al-Ansari, who said: I set out with my father to Medina on some business, and that was the first time the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was mentioned in Mecca. Night overtook us at the shepherd of a flock. When half the night had passed, a wolf came and took a lamb from the flock. The shepherd leaped up and said: O lord of the valley, I am your protected one. Then a caller called out: O Sirhan, release it! The lamb came running until it entered the flock. And God revealed to His Messenger in Mecca: ﴿And that men of mankind used to seek refuge with men of the jinn﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾, that he said: sin.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: In the Jahiliyya, when people alighted in a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil that is in it. So nothing is more fond of them than that. That is His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The devils had seats in the heaven where they heard revelation. When they heard a word, they added nine to it. The word itself would be true, but what they added would be false. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were prevented from their seats. They mentioned that to Iblis, and before that the stars had not been thrown. He said to them: This is nothing but a matter that has occurred on the earth. So he sent his armies, and they found the Messenger of God (ﷺ) standing praying between two mountains in Mecca. They came to him and informed him. He said: This is the event that has occurred on the earth.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His words: ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, he said: Among us is the Muslim, and among us is the polytheist. And ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾: different desires.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿So he will fear neither loss nor oppression﴾, that he said: He will not fear a deficiency in his good deeds nor an increase in his evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: this is the consensus (fi qawl al-jami').
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Surat al-Jinn was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'ishah and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "Uhiya" in the quadriliteral form (ruba'iyyan).
Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn Iyas and al-'Ataki from Abu 'Amr read "Wuhiya" in the triliteral form (thulathiyyan), and both are dialectal variants (lughatan).

There is a disagreement over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw them or did not see them. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that he did not see them, because the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, to your community: It has been revealed to me through Jibril ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾. What supports this is what is established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them.

'Ikrimah said: The surah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq]. The matter was mentioned in Surat al-Ahqaf with what gives further benefit on this.

His saying: ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾: this is the substitute for the subject (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il), and for this reason "anna" is pronounced with a fatha, and the pronoun is for the matter (li-l-sha'n). According to the Kufis and al-Akhfash, it is permissible that the substitute for the subject be the prepositional phrase. Al-Nafar is a noun for a group ranging from three to ten.

Al-Dahhak said: The jinn are the offspring of the jann, and they are not shayatin (devils).
Al-Hasan said: They are the offspring of Iblis.
It has been said they are hidden rational bodies in which the fiery and airy natures predominate; it has been said they are a kind of disembodied spirits; and it has been said they are human souls separated from their bodies.

The scholars have differed on whether believing jinn enter Paradise, just as their disobedient ones enter the Fire, based on His saying in Surat Tabarak: ﴿And We made them missiles against the devils, and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], and the saying of the jinn later in this surah: ﴿And as for the deviators, they have become fuel for Hell﴾, and other verses. Al-Hasan said: they enter Paradise. Mujahid said: they do not enter it, even if they are turned away from the Fire.

The first view is more preferable, because of His saying in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿Neither man nor jinn had touched them before﴾, and there are verses in Surat al-Rahman other than this that indicate that; so refer to them. We have already stated that the truth is that Allah did not send to them messengers from among themselves; rather all the messengers were from mankind. Even if His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-Zumar: 71] seems to indicate otherwise, its apparent meaning is refuted by many verses in the Mighty Book indicating that Allah the Glorified did not send messengers except from the children of Adam. These discussions would be lengthy; the aim here is to indicate in the briefest expression.

﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, i.e., they said to their people when they returned to them: We heard a recited speech that is wondrous in its eloquence and rhetoric. It has been said: wondrous in its admonitions; it has been said: in its blessing. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun described with it for emphasis, or by omitting a modifier: i.e., "possessing wonder," or the verbal noun in the sense of the active participle: i.e., "amazing."

﴿It guides to righteousness﴾, i.e., to the right paths of affairs, which are truth and correctness. It has been said: to the knowledge of Allah. This clause is another description of the Qur'an. ﴿So we have believed in it﴾, i.e., we affirmed it as being from Allah. ﴿And we will never associate with our Lord anyone﴾ from His creation, nor take with Him another god, because He is the sole possessor of lordship. In this is a rebuke to the disbelievers among the children of Adam, since the jinn believed by hearing the Qur'an only once and benefited from hearing a few verses of it, and by their intellects they perceived that it is the speech of Allah and believed in it, while the disbelievers of mankind, especially their leaders and their great ones, did not benefit from hearing it many times and from its recitation to them at various times, together with the Messenger being from among them reciting it to them in their own tongue. Indeed, Allah overthrew them in the most humiliating downfall (p-1538) and killed them in the most shameful killing; and the punishment of the Hereafter is severer, if only they knew.

﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, 'Alqamah, Yahya ibn Wthab, al-A'mash, Khalaf and al-Sulami read ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ with a fatha on "anna", and likewise they read what follows it that is coordinated with it, eleven places up to His saying: ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾. The rest read with a kasra in all these places, except His saying: ﴿and that the mosques are for Allah﴾, where they all agreed on the fatha. As for the one who reads with a fatha in these places, it is by coordination with the position (mahall) of the prepositional phrase in ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾, as if it were said: "so we affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord," etc. As for the one who reads with a kasra in these places, it is by coordination with ﴿Indeed we have heard﴾: "So they said: Indeed we have heard a Qur'an," and they said that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, to the end.

Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading with the kasra, because all of it is from the speech of the jinn and is reported from them by His saying ﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard﴾.

Abu Ja'far and Shu'bah read with the fatha in three places, namely: ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾,
﴿and that it was that our foolish one used to say﴾,
﴿and that there were men from mankind﴾.
They said: because it is from the revelation (min al-wahy), and they read the rest with a kasra, because it is from the speech of the jinn.

The Jumhur read ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾ with the fatha, because it is coordinated with His saying: "that it listened."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Shaybah, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read with the kasra in this place, coordinated with ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾ under that earlier estimation. They agreed on the fatha in ﴿annahu istama'a﴾, as they agreed on the fatha in "anna al-masajid" and in ﴿law istaqamu﴾, and they agreed on the kasra in ﴿fa-qalu inna sami'na﴾, ﴿qul innama ad'u rabbi﴾, ﴿qul in adri﴾, and ﴿qul inni la amliku lakum﴾.

The "jadd" (majesty) according to the linguists is greatness and grandeur; one says "jadda fi 'aini," i.e., it became great in my eye. So the meaning: the greatness and majesty of our Lord is exalted. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid.

al-Hasan said: The intended meaning is His exalted wealth (ghina), and from this it is said of luck "jadd," and a man is "majdud," i.e., fortunate. In the hadith: "and wealth does not benefit the possessor of wealth (dha al-jadd) against You the wealth" — Abu 'Ubayd and al-Khalil said: i.e., wealth does not benefit the rich against You the riches; rather it is obedience that benefits him. Al-Qurtubi and al-Dahhak said: His jadd is His blessings and favors upon His creation.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: His dominion and authority.

al-Suddi said: His command.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾: i.e., exalted is our Lord. It has been said: His jadd is His power.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Allah has no jadd, and the jinn only said it out of ignorance.

The Jumhur read "jadd" with a fatha on the jim. 'Ikrimah, Abu Haywah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a kasra on the jim, which is the opposite of jest. Abu al-Ashhab read "jaddayi rabbina," i.e., its bounty and benefit.

It is also related from 'Ikrimah that he read with tanwin on "jaddun" and a raf' on "rabbuna," as a substitute (badal) for "jaddun."

﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾: this is an explanation of the exaltedness of His jadd, glory be to Him.

al-Zajjaj said: Exalted is the majesty and greatness of our Lord above taking a consort or a son. It seems the jinn, by this, alerted to the error of the disbelievers who attribute to Allah a consort and a son, and they declared Allah, glorified be He, free of both.

﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say about Allah an excessive lie (shatatan)﴾. The pronoun in "annahu" refers to the matter or the affair, and "safihuna" may be the subject of "kana," with "yaqulu" as the predicate; or "safihuna" may be the agent of "yaqulu," and the clause is the predicate of "kana," whose noun is a pronoun referring to the matter or the affair.

It is also permissible that "kana" be redundant (za'idah). By "their foolish one" they mean their disobedient ones and their polytheists.

Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Qatadah said: they meant by it Iblis. "Shatat" is excess in disbelief.

Abu Malik said: it is injustice (jawr). al-Kalbi said: it is lying. Its origin is deviation from the intended course and exceeding the limit.

From this is the poet's saying:
"In whatever condition they judged you, they went to excess, and that was only because the Wakhst directed you there."

﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never say a lie against Allah﴾, i.e., we reckoned that mankind and the jinn would not lie against Allah by claiming He has a partner, a consort and a son; therefore we believed them in that until we heard the Qur'an, and we knew the falsehood of their saying and the falsehood of what we used to suppose of them regarding truthfulness. The accusative of "kadhiban" is either a verbal noun emphasizing "yaqulu," since lying is a type of speech, or an adjective of a deleted verbal noun: i.e., "a lying speech."

Ya'qub, al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "an lan taqula" from "al-taqawwul," so that on this reading "kadhiban" is the direct object.

﴿And that there were men from mankind who used to seek refuge with men from the jinn﴾. al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: When an Arab man arrived at a valley, he would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people." So he would spend the night under his protection until morning, and this verse was revealed.

Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then from Banu Hanifah, then this spread among the Arabs; when Islam came, they sought refuge with Allah and abandoned them. ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾: i.e., the men of the jinn increased those who sought refuge with them from the men of mankind in rahaq, i.e., foolishness and transgression, i.e., arrogance and insolence; or those among mankind who sought refuge increased those they sought refuge with from the men of the jinn in rahaq, because those sought-refuge-with would say, "We have become lords over the jinn and mankind."

Mujahid and Qatadah said the first; Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said the second.

In the speech of the Arabs, "rahaq" means sin and the committing of forbidden things, and a man is "rahiq" if he is so; from this is His saying "tarhaquhum dhillatun" (humiliation will cover them), i.e., covers them. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:
"Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; does a lover find relief if he has not been struck by rahaq?"
meaning sin.

It has been said rahaq is fear, i.e., the jinn increased mankind in fear through this seeking of refuge with them. It has also been said that a man of mankind would say, "I seek refuge with so-and-so from the chiefs of the Arabs, from the jinn of this valley." This is supported by what has been said, that the word "rijal" is not applied to the jinn; so His saying "bi-rijalin" would be a description of those they seek refuge with from the men of mankind, i.e., they seek refuge with them from the evil of the jinn. This is far-fetched; and applying the word "rijal" to the jinn, even granting it is not linguistically correct, there is no barrier to applying it to them here by way of symmetry (mushakalah).

﴿And that they thought as you thought that Allah would never raise anyone﴾. This is from the speech of the jinn to mankind: i.e., and the jinn thought, as you, O mankind, thought, that there is no resurrection.

It has been said the meaning is: and mankind thought, as you, O jinn, thought, i.e., they do not believe in resurrection just as you do not believe.

﴿And that we touched the sky﴾. This is also from the speech of the jinn: i.e., we sought news, as our custom had been with it. ﴿Then we found it filled with a strong guard﴾ of angels guarding it against eavesdropping. "Harasan" is the plural of "haris" (guard), and "shadidan" is a description of "harasan": i.e., powerful; and "shuhuban" is the plural of "shihab," which is the flame drawn from the fire of a star, as its explanation was previously given in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We made them missiles for the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. The position of His saying "mulli'at harasan shadidan" is accusative, as the second object of "wajadna," since it is transitive to two objects; it is also permissible that it be transitive to one object, in which case the clause's position is accusative as a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, and "harasan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Its description with the singular is considered in terms of the wording, as one says "al-salaf al-salih," i.e., the righteous predecessors.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 72, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen﴾: that is, we, the company of the jinn, before this used to sit in the heavens on seats to listen, meaning places in which we sat to eavesdrop on news from the heavens. "Li-l-sam'" means seats existing for listening. "Maqā'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a noun of place. The rebellious jinn used to do this in order to hear news of the heavens from the angels and then convey it to the soothsayers (kahana). So God, exalted is He, guarded it by sending His Messenger (ﷺ) with flaming shooting stars. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿But whoever now listens will find a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾, that is, one is posted for him to be struck with it, or it is posted because of him to prevent him from listening. His words "al-'āna" (now) is a adverb of the present, and it is used figuratively for the future. The accusative of "rasadan" (lying in wait) is either as an attribute of "shihāban" (flame) or as an object of purpose. It is singular, but it may also be a collective noun like "al-haras" (the guard).

They have disagreed over whether the devils were struck with flames before the mission (al-mab'ath) or not. A group said: that did not happen.

Al-Wahidi related from Ma'mar, who said: I said to al-Zuhri: Were the stars thrown in the Jahiliyya? He said: Yes. I said: What do you think of His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in it﴾ and so on? He said: Its matter was made severe and intensified when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent.

Ibn Qutayba said: Stoning had occurred before his mission, but it was not like it in its severity of guarding after his mission. They used to steal some news in certain circumstances, but when he was sent they were prevented from that entirely.

'Abd al-Malik ibn Sabur said: The heavens were not guarded during the fatra (the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad). When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the heavens were guarded, the devils were struck with flames, and they were prevented from approaching the heaven.

Nafi' ibn Jubayr said: During the fatra, the devils used to listen and were not struck. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were struck with flames. The discussion of this has already preceded.

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾: that is, we do not know whether evil is intended for the people of the earth because of this guarding of the heaven, or whether their Lord intends for them rashad (guidance), that is, good.

Ibn Zayd said: Iblis said: We do not know whether God intended by this prevention to send down a punishment upon the people of the earth, or to send to them a messenger.

The word "sharrun" (evil) is in the nominative either by the construction of "ishtighāl" (the verb being occupied with the object, i.e., a verb governing a pronoun) or as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is what follows. The first is more preferable. The clause fills the place of the two objects of "nadri" (we know). The more appropriate view is that this is the speech of the jinn among themselves, not the speech of Iblis as Ibn Zayd said.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: that is, some said to others, when they called their companions to faith in Muhammad (ﷺ): We, before hearing the Qur'an, were among those described as righteous. ﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, a people below that, meaning below those described as righteous. It has been said that by "the righteous" he meant the believers, and by "those below that" the disbelievers. The first is more preferable.

The meaning of ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾ is: groups scattered apart and varied kinds. "Qidad" is the plural of "qidda," which is a piece of a thing. A people became "qidad" when their conditions became dispersed. From this is the poet's saying:

The one who holds back and extends, guiding to His obedience,
Amid the trials of people when their desires are scattered (qidad).

The meaning is: we were people of divergent paths, or our paths were divergent, or we were like divergent paths. From this is Labid's saying:

The eye did not reach all its desire
On the day the horses walk in scattered ranks (bi-l-qidad).

And his saying also:

And I said, while Zayd was bare-headed,
On the day the horses of 'Amr turned in scattered flight (qidadan).

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: they were different religions. Qatada said: they were divergent desires.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: They were Muslims, Jews, Christians, and Magians. Mujahid said the same.

Al-Hasan said: The jinn are like you, Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on faith), Rafida (those who reject the early caliphs), and Shi'a (partisans). Al-Suddi said the same.

﴿And that we thought that we would never escape God in the earth﴾: here "zanan" (thought) means knowledge and certainty. That is: we knew that the matter is that we will never escape God in the earth, wherever we are in it, nor will we outrun Him if He intends a matter for us. ﴿And we will never escape Him by fleeing﴾: that is, fleeing from it; so it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿we believed in it﴾, and we affirmed that it is from God, and we did not deny it as the disbelieving humans denied it. ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither loss (bakhsan) nor oppression (rahaqan)﴾: that is, he will not fear a deficiency in his deed and its reward, nor injustice and something hateful that covers him. "Bakhs" is deficiency, and "rahaq" is transgression and insolence. The meaning is: he will not fear that any of his good deeds will be diminished or that his evil deeds will be increased. The explanation of "rahaq" has already been given shortly before.

The majority recited "bakhsan" with a sukun on the kha'. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it with a fatha on it. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash recited "fa-lā yakhaf" (with a jussive) as an answer to the conditional, but there is no basis for this after the entry of the fa'. The implied meaning is: "fa-huwa lā yakhāf" (so he does not fear), and the matter is clear.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out with a group of his companions, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and the devils had been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars were sent against them. The devils returned to their people, and they said: What is wrong with you? They said: We have been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars have been sent against us. They said: Nothing has come between you and the news of the heaven except something that has happened. So strike the eastern and western parts of the earth, so that you may know what this matter is that has come between you and the news of the heaven. Those who had headed toward Tihama returned to the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was at Nakhla, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and he was leading his companions in the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an, they listened to it and said: By God, this is what has come between you and the news of the heaven. At that moment, when they returned to their people, they said: O our people, ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, ﴿It guides to righteousness, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. Then God revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾." What was revealed to him was the speech of the jinn.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾, that he said: They were from the jinn of Nasibin.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord﴾, that he said: His blessings and His greatness.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: His command and His power.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated (al-Suyuti said with a weak chain) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), concerning His words: ﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say﴾, that he said: It is Iblis.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa', al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ikrima ibn Abi al-Sa'ib al-Ansari, who said: I set out with my father to Medina on some business, and that was the first time the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was mentioned in Mecca. Night overtook us at the shepherd of a flock. When half the night had passed, a wolf came and took a lamb from the flock. The shepherd leaped up and said: O lord of the valley, I am your protected one. Then a caller called out: O Sirhan, release it! The lamb came running until it entered the flock. And God revealed to His Messenger in Mecca: ﴿And that men of mankind used to seek refuge with men of the jinn﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾, that he said: sin.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: In the Jahiliyya, when people alighted in a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil that is in it. So nothing is more fond of them than that. That is His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The devils had seats in the heaven where they heard revelation. When they heard a word, they added nine to it. The word itself would be true, but what they added would be false. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were prevented from their seats. They mentioned that to Iblis, and before that the stars had not been thrown. He said to them: This is nothing but a matter that has occurred on the earth. So he sent his armies, and they found the Messenger of God (ﷺ) standing praying between two mountains in Mecca. They came to him and informed him. He said: This is the event that has occurred on the earth.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His words: ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, he said: Among us is the Muslim, and among us is the polytheist. And ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾: different desires.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿So he will fear neither loss nor oppression﴾, that he said: He will not fear a deficiency in his good deeds nor an increase in his evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: this is the consensus (fi qawl al-jami').
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Surat al-Jinn was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'ishah and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "Uhiya" in the quadriliteral form (ruba'iyyan).
Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn Iyas and al-'Ataki from Abu 'Amr read "Wuhiya" in the triliteral form (thulathiyyan), and both are dialectal variants (lughatan).

There is a disagreement over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw them or did not see them. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that he did not see them, because the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, to your community: It has been revealed to me through Jibril ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾. What supports this is what is established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them.

'Ikrimah said: The surah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq]. The matter was mentioned in Surat al-Ahqaf with what gives further benefit on this.

His saying: ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾: this is the substitute for the subject (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il), and for this reason "anna" is pronounced with a fatha, and the pronoun is for the matter (li-l-sha'n). According to the Kufis and al-Akhfash, it is permissible that the substitute for the subject be the prepositional phrase. Al-Nafar is a noun for a group ranging from three to ten.

Al-Dahhak said: The jinn are the offspring of the jann, and they are not shayatin (devils).
Al-Hasan said: They are the offspring of Iblis.
It has been said they are hidden rational bodies in which the fiery and airy natures predominate; it has been said they are a kind of disembodied spirits; and it has been said they are human souls separated from their bodies.

The scholars have differed on whether believing jinn enter Paradise, just as their disobedient ones enter the Fire, based on His saying in Surat Tabarak: ﴿And We made them missiles against the devils, and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], and the saying of the jinn later in this surah: ﴿And as for the deviators, they have become fuel for Hell﴾, and other verses. Al-Hasan said: they enter Paradise. Mujahid said: they do not enter it, even if they are turned away from the Fire.

The first view is more preferable, because of His saying in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿Neither man nor jinn had touched them before﴾, and there are verses in Surat al-Rahman other than this that indicate that; so refer to them. We have already stated that the truth is that Allah did not send to them messengers from among themselves; rather all the messengers were from mankind. Even if His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-Zumar: 71] seems to indicate otherwise, its apparent meaning is refuted by many verses in the Mighty Book indicating that Allah the Glorified did not send messengers except from the children of Adam. These discussions would be lengthy; the aim here is to indicate in the briefest expression.

﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, i.e., they said to their people when they returned to them: We heard a recited speech that is wondrous in its eloquence and rhetoric. It has been said: wondrous in its admonitions; it has been said: in its blessing. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun described with it for emphasis, or by omitting a modifier: i.e., "possessing wonder," or the verbal noun in the sense of the active participle: i.e., "amazing."

﴿It guides to righteousness﴾, i.e., to the right paths of affairs, which are truth and correctness. It has been said: to the knowledge of Allah. This clause is another description of the Qur'an. ﴿So we have believed in it﴾, i.e., we affirmed it as being from Allah. ﴿And we will never associate with our Lord anyone﴾ from His creation, nor take with Him another god, because He is the sole possessor of lordship. In this is a rebuke to the disbelievers among the children of Adam, since the jinn believed by hearing the Qur'an only once and benefited from hearing a few verses of it, and by their intellects they perceived that it is the speech of Allah and believed in it, while the disbelievers of mankind, especially their leaders and their great ones, did not benefit from hearing it many times and from its recitation to them at various times, together with the Messenger being from among them reciting it to them in their own tongue. Indeed, Allah overthrew them in the most humiliating downfall (p-1538) and killed them in the most shameful killing; and the punishment of the Hereafter is severer, if only they knew.

﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, 'Alqamah, Yahya ibn Wthab, al-A'mash, Khalaf and al-Sulami read ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ with a fatha on "anna", and likewise they read what follows it that is coordinated with it, eleven places up to His saying: ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾. The rest read with a kasra in all these places, except His saying: ﴿and that the mosques are for Allah﴾, where they all agreed on the fatha. As for the one who reads with a fatha in these places, it is by coordination with the position (mahall) of the prepositional phrase in ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾, as if it were said: "so we affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord," etc. As for the one who reads with a kasra in these places, it is by coordination with ﴿Indeed we have heard﴾: "So they said: Indeed we have heard a Qur'an," and they said that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, to the end.

Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading with the kasra, because all of it is from the speech of the jinn and is reported from them by His saying ﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard﴾.

Abu Ja'far and Shu'bah read with the fatha in three places, namely: ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾,
﴿and that it was that our foolish one used to say﴾,
﴿and that there were men from mankind﴾.
They said: because it is from the revelation (min al-wahy), and they read the rest with a kasra, because it is from the speech of the jinn.

The Jumhur read ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾ with the fatha, because it is coordinated with His saying: "that it listened."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Shaybah, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read with the kasra in this place, coordinated with ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾ under that earlier estimation. They agreed on the fatha in ﴿annahu istama'a﴾, as they agreed on the fatha in "anna al-masajid" and in ﴿law istaqamu﴾, and they agreed on the kasra in ﴿fa-qalu inna sami'na﴾, ﴿qul innama ad'u rabbi﴾, ﴿qul in adri﴾, and ﴿qul inni la amliku lakum﴾.

The "jadd" (majesty) according to the linguists is greatness and grandeur; one says "jadda fi 'aini," i.e., it became great in my eye. So the meaning: the greatness and majesty of our Lord is exalted. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid.

al-Hasan said: The intended meaning is His exalted wealth (ghina), and from this it is said of luck "jadd," and a man is "majdud," i.e., fortunate. In the hadith: "and wealth does not benefit the possessor of wealth (dha al-jadd) against You the wealth" — Abu 'Ubayd and al-Khalil said: i.e., wealth does not benefit the rich against You the riches; rather it is obedience that benefits him. Al-Qurtubi and al-Dahhak said: His jadd is His blessings and favors upon His creation.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: His dominion and authority.

al-Suddi said: His command.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾: i.e., exalted is our Lord. It has been said: His jadd is His power.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Allah has no jadd, and the jinn only said it out of ignorance.

The Jumhur read "jadd" with a fatha on the jim. 'Ikrimah, Abu Haywah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a kasra on the jim, which is the opposite of jest. Abu al-Ashhab read "jaddayi rabbina," i.e., its bounty and benefit.

It is also related from 'Ikrimah that he read with tanwin on "jaddun" and a raf' on "rabbuna," as a substitute (badal) for "jaddun."

﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾: this is an explanation of the exaltedness of His jadd, glory be to Him.

al-Zajjaj said: Exalted is the majesty and greatness of our Lord above taking a consort or a son. It seems the jinn, by this, alerted to the error of the disbelievers who attribute to Allah a consort and a son, and they declared Allah, glorified be He, free of both.

﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say about Allah an excessive lie (shatatan)﴾. The pronoun in "annahu" refers to the matter or the affair, and "safihuna" may be the subject of "kana," with "yaqulu" as the predicate; or "safihuna" may be the agent of "yaqulu," and the clause is the predicate of "kana," whose noun is a pronoun referring to the matter or the affair.

It is also permissible that "kana" be redundant (za'idah). By "their foolish one" they mean their disobedient ones and their polytheists.

Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Qatadah said: they meant by it Iblis. "Shatat" is excess in disbelief.

Abu Malik said: it is injustice (jawr). al-Kalbi said: it is lying. Its origin is deviation from the intended course and exceeding the limit.

From this is the poet's saying:
"In whatever condition they judged you, they went to excess, and that was only because the Wakhst directed you there."

﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never say a lie against Allah﴾, i.e., we reckoned that mankind and the jinn would not lie against Allah by claiming He has a partner, a consort and a son; therefore we believed them in that until we heard the Qur'an, and we knew the falsehood of their saying and the falsehood of what we used to suppose of them regarding truthfulness. The accusative of "kadhiban" is either a verbal noun emphasizing "yaqulu," since lying is a type of speech, or an adjective of a deleted verbal noun: i.e., "a lying speech."

Ya'qub, al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "an lan taqula" from "al-taqawwul," so that on this reading "kadhiban" is the direct object.

﴿And that there were men from mankind who used to seek refuge with men from the jinn﴾. al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: When an Arab man arrived at a valley, he would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people." So he would spend the night under his protection until morning, and this verse was revealed.

Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then from Banu Hanifah, then this spread among the Arabs; when Islam came, they sought refuge with Allah and abandoned them. ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾: i.e., the men of the jinn increased those who sought refuge with them from the men of mankind in rahaq, i.e., foolishness and transgression, i.e., arrogance and insolence; or those among mankind who sought refuge increased those they sought refuge with from the men of the jinn in rahaq, because those sought-refuge-with would say, "We have become lords over the jinn and mankind."

Mujahid and Qatadah said the first; Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said the second.

In the speech of the Arabs, "rahaq" means sin and the committing of forbidden things, and a man is "rahiq" if he is so; from this is His saying "tarhaquhum dhillatun" (humiliation will cover them), i.e., covers them. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:
"Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; does a lover find relief if he has not been struck by rahaq?"
meaning sin.

It has been said rahaq is fear, i.e., the jinn increased mankind in fear through this seeking of refuge with them. It has also been said that a man of mankind would say, "I seek refuge with so-and-so from the chiefs of the Arabs, from the jinn of this valley." This is supported by what has been said, that the word "rijal" is not applied to the jinn; so His saying "bi-rijalin" would be a description of those they seek refuge with from the men of mankind, i.e., they seek refuge with them from the evil of the jinn. This is far-fetched; and applying the word "rijal" to the jinn, even granting it is not linguistically correct, there is no barrier to applying it to them here by way of symmetry (mushakalah).

﴿And that they thought as you thought that Allah would never raise anyone﴾. This is from the speech of the jinn to mankind: i.e., and the jinn thought, as you, O mankind, thought, that there is no resurrection.

It has been said the meaning is: and mankind thought, as you, O jinn, thought, i.e., they do not believe in resurrection just as you do not believe.

﴿And that we touched the sky﴾. This is also from the speech of the jinn: i.e., we sought news, as our custom had been with it. ﴿Then we found it filled with a strong guard﴾ of angels guarding it against eavesdropping. "Harasan" is the plural of "haris" (guard), and "shadidan" is a description of "harasan": i.e., powerful; and "shuhuban" is the plural of "shihab," which is the flame drawn from the fire of a star, as its explanation was previously given in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We made them missiles for the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. The position of His saying "mulli'at harasan shadidan" is accusative, as the second object of "wajadna," since it is transitive to two objects; it is also permissible that it be transitive to one object, in which case the clause's position is accusative as a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, and "harasan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Its description with the singular is considered in terms of the wording, as one says "al-salaf al-salih," i.e., the righteous predecessors.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 72, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen﴾: that is, we, the company of the jinn, before this used to sit in the heavens on seats to listen, meaning places in which we sat to eavesdrop on news from the heavens. "Li-l-sam'" means seats existing for listening. "Maqā'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a noun of place. The rebellious jinn used to do this in order to hear news of the heavens from the angels and then convey it to the soothsayers (kahana). So God, exalted is He, guarded it by sending His Messenger (ﷺ) with flaming shooting stars. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿But whoever now listens will find a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾, that is, one is posted for him to be struck with it, or it is posted because of him to prevent him from listening. His words "al-'āna" (now) is a adverb of the present, and it is used figuratively for the future. The accusative of "rasadan" (lying in wait) is either as an attribute of "shihāban" (flame) or as an object of purpose. It is singular, but it may also be a collective noun like "al-haras" (the guard).

They have disagreed over whether the devils were struck with flames before the mission (al-mab'ath) or not. A group said: that did not happen.

Al-Wahidi related from Ma'mar, who said: I said to al-Zuhri: Were the stars thrown in the Jahiliyya? He said: Yes. I said: What do you think of His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in it﴾ and so on? He said: Its matter was made severe and intensified when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent.

Ibn Qutayba said: Stoning had occurred before his mission, but it was not like it in its severity of guarding after his mission. They used to steal some news in certain circumstances, but when he was sent they were prevented from that entirely.

'Abd al-Malik ibn Sabur said: The heavens were not guarded during the fatra (the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad). When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the heavens were guarded, the devils were struck with flames, and they were prevented from approaching the heaven.

Nafi' ibn Jubayr said: During the fatra, the devils used to listen and were not struck. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were struck with flames. The discussion of this has already preceded.

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾: that is, we do not know whether evil is intended for the people of the earth because of this guarding of the heaven, or whether their Lord intends for them rashad (guidance), that is, good.

Ibn Zayd said: Iblis said: We do not know whether God intended by this prevention to send down a punishment upon the people of the earth, or to send to them a messenger.

The word "sharrun" (evil) is in the nominative either by the construction of "ishtighāl" (the verb being occupied with the object, i.e., a verb governing a pronoun) or as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is what follows. The first is more preferable. The clause fills the place of the two objects of "nadri" (we know). The more appropriate view is that this is the speech of the jinn among themselves, not the speech of Iblis as Ibn Zayd said.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: that is, some said to others, when they called their companions to faith in Muhammad (ﷺ): We, before hearing the Qur'an, were among those described as righteous. ﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, a people below that, meaning below those described as righteous. It has been said that by "the righteous" he meant the believers, and by "those below that" the disbelievers. The first is more preferable.

The meaning of ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾ is: groups scattered apart and varied kinds. "Qidad" is the plural of "qidda," which is a piece of a thing. A people became "qidad" when their conditions became dispersed. From this is the poet's saying:

The one who holds back and extends, guiding to His obedience,
Amid the trials of people when their desires are scattered (qidad).

The meaning is: we were people of divergent paths, or our paths were divergent, or we were like divergent paths. From this is Labid's saying:

The eye did not reach all its desire
On the day the horses walk in scattered ranks (bi-l-qidad).

And his saying also:

And I said, while Zayd was bare-headed,
On the day the horses of 'Amr turned in scattered flight (qidadan).

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: they were different religions. Qatada said: they were divergent desires.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: They were Muslims, Jews, Christians, and Magians. Mujahid said the same.

Al-Hasan said: The jinn are like you, Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on faith), Rafida (those who reject the early caliphs), and Shi'a (partisans). Al-Suddi said the same.

﴿And that we thought that we would never escape God in the earth﴾: here "zanan" (thought) means knowledge and certainty. That is: we knew that the matter is that we will never escape God in the earth, wherever we are in it, nor will we outrun Him if He intends a matter for us. ﴿And we will never escape Him by fleeing﴾: that is, fleeing from it; so it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿we believed in it﴾, and we affirmed that it is from God, and we did not deny it as the disbelieving humans denied it. ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither loss (bakhsan) nor oppression (rahaqan)﴾: that is, he will not fear a deficiency in his deed and its reward, nor injustice and something hateful that covers him. "Bakhs" is deficiency, and "rahaq" is transgression and insolence. The meaning is: he will not fear that any of his good deeds will be diminished or that his evil deeds will be increased. The explanation of "rahaq" has already been given shortly before.

The majority recited "bakhsan" with a sukun on the kha'. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it with a fatha on it. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash recited "fa-lā yakhaf" (with a jussive) as an answer to the conditional, but there is no basis for this after the entry of the fa'. The implied meaning is: "fa-huwa lā yakhāf" (so he does not fear), and the matter is clear.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out with a group of his companions, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and the devils had been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars were sent against them. The devils returned to their people, and they said: What is wrong with you? They said: We have been prevented from the news of the heaven, and flaming stars have been sent against us. They said: Nothing has come between you and the news of the heaven except something that has happened. So strike the eastern and western parts of the earth, so that you may know what this matter is that has come between you and the news of the heaven. Those who had headed toward Tihama returned to the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was at Nakhla, intending the market of 'Ukaz, and he was leading his companions in the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an, they listened to it and said: By God, this is what has come between you and the news of the heaven. At that moment, when they returned to their people, they said: O our people, ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, ﴿It guides to righteousness, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. Then God revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾." What was revealed to him was the speech of the jinn.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾, that he said: They were from the jinn of Nasibin.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord﴾, that he said: His blessings and His greatness.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: His command and His power.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated (al-Suyuti said with a weak chain) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), concerning His words: ﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say﴾, that he said: It is Iblis.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa', al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ikrima ibn Abi al-Sa'ib al-Ansari, who said: I set out with my father to Medina on some business, and that was the first time the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was mentioned in Mecca. Night overtook us at the shepherd of a flock. When half the night had passed, a wolf came and took a lamb from the flock. The shepherd leaped up and said: O lord of the valley, I am your protected one. Then a caller called out: O Sirhan, release it! The lamb came running until it entered the flock. And God revealed to His Messenger in Mecca: ﴿And that men of mankind used to seek refuge with men of the jinn﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾, that he said: sin.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: In the Jahiliyya, when people alighted in a valley, they would say: We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil that is in it. So nothing is more fond of them than that. That is His words: ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The devils had seats in the heaven where they heard revelation. When they heard a word, they added nine to it. The word itself would be true, but what they added would be false. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were prevented from their seats. They mentioned that to Iblis, and before that the stars had not been thrown. He said to them: This is nothing but a matter that has occurred on the earth. So he sent his armies, and they found the Messenger of God (ﷺ) standing praying between two mountains in Mecca. They came to him and informed him. He said: This is the event that has occurred on the earth.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His words: ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, he said: Among us is the Muslim, and among us is the polytheist. And ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾: different desires.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿So he will fear neither loss nor oppression﴾, that he said: He will not fear a deficiency in his good deeds nor an increase in his evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: this is the consensus (fi qawl al-jami').
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Surat al-Jinn was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'ishah and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "Uhiya" in the quadriliteral form (ruba'iyyan).
Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn Iyas and al-'Ataki from Abu 'Amr read "Wuhiya" in the triliteral form (thulathiyyan), and both are dialectal variants (lughatan).

There is a disagreement over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw them or did not see them. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that he did not see them, because the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, to your community: It has been revealed to me through Jibril ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾. What supports this is what is established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them.

'Ikrimah said: The surah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq]. The matter was mentioned in Surat al-Ahqaf with what gives further benefit on this.

His saying: ﴿that a group of the jinn listened﴾: this is the substitute for the subject (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il), and for this reason "anna" is pronounced with a fatha, and the pronoun is for the matter (li-l-sha'n). According to the Kufis and al-Akhfash, it is permissible that the substitute for the subject be the prepositional phrase. Al-Nafar is a noun for a group ranging from three to ten.

Al-Dahhak said: The jinn are the offspring of the jann, and they are not shayatin (devils).
Al-Hasan said: They are the offspring of Iblis.
It has been said they are hidden rational bodies in which the fiery and airy natures predominate; it has been said they are a kind of disembodied spirits; and it has been said they are human souls separated from their bodies.

The scholars have differed on whether believing jinn enter Paradise, just as their disobedient ones enter the Fire, based on His saying in Surat Tabarak: ﴿And We made them missiles against the devils, and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], and the saying of the jinn later in this surah: ﴿And as for the deviators, they have become fuel for Hell﴾, and other verses. Al-Hasan said: they enter Paradise. Mujahid said: they do not enter it, even if they are turned away from the Fire.

The first view is more preferable, because of His saying in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿Neither man nor jinn had touched them before﴾, and there are verses in Surat al-Rahman other than this that indicate that; so refer to them. We have already stated that the truth is that Allah did not send to them messengers from among themselves; rather all the messengers were from mankind. Even if His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-Zumar: 71] seems to indicate otherwise, its apparent meaning is refuted by many verses in the Mighty Book indicating that Allah the Glorified did not send messengers except from the children of Adam. These discussions would be lengthy; the aim here is to indicate in the briefest expression.

﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, i.e., they said to their people when they returned to them: We heard a recited speech that is wondrous in its eloquence and rhetoric. It has been said: wondrous in its admonitions; it has been said: in its blessing. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun described with it for emphasis, or by omitting a modifier: i.e., "possessing wonder," or the verbal noun in the sense of the active participle: i.e., "amazing."

﴿It guides to righteousness﴾, i.e., to the right paths of affairs, which are truth and correctness. It has been said: to the knowledge of Allah. This clause is another description of the Qur'an. ﴿So we have believed in it﴾, i.e., we affirmed it as being from Allah. ﴿And we will never associate with our Lord anyone﴾ from His creation, nor take with Him another god, because He is the sole possessor of lordship. In this is a rebuke to the disbelievers among the children of Adam, since the jinn believed by hearing the Qur'an only once and benefited from hearing a few verses of it, and by their intellects they perceived that it is the speech of Allah and believed in it, while the disbelievers of mankind, especially their leaders and their great ones, did not benefit from hearing it many times and from its recitation to them at various times, together with the Messenger being from among them reciting it to them in their own tongue. Indeed, Allah overthrew them in the most humiliating downfall (p-1538) and killed them in the most shameful killing; and the punishment of the Hereafter is severer, if only they knew.

﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, 'Alqamah, Yahya ibn Wthab, al-A'mash, Khalaf and al-Sulami read ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ with a fatha on "anna", and likewise they read what follows it that is coordinated with it, eleven places up to His saying: ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾. The rest read with a kasra in all these places, except His saying: ﴿and that the mosques are for Allah﴾, where they all agreed on the fatha. As for the one who reads with a fatha in these places, it is by coordination with the position (mahall) of the prepositional phrase in ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾, as if it were said: "so we affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord," etc. As for the one who reads with a kasra in these places, it is by coordination with ﴿Indeed we have heard﴾: "So they said: Indeed we have heard a Qur'an," and they said that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, to the end.

Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading with the kasra, because all of it is from the speech of the jinn and is reported from them by His saying ﴿So they said: Indeed we have heard﴾.

Abu Ja'far and Shu'bah read with the fatha in three places, namely: ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾,
﴿and that it was that our foolish one used to say﴾,
﴿and that there were men from mankind﴾.
They said: because it is from the revelation (min al-wahy), and they read the rest with a kasra, because it is from the speech of the jinn.

The Jumhur read ﴿and that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾ with the fatha, because it is coordinated with His saying: "that it listened."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Shaybah, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read with the kasra in this place, coordinated with ﴿fa-amanna bihi﴾ under that earlier estimation. They agreed on the fatha in ﴿annahu istama'a﴾, as they agreed on the fatha in "anna al-masajid" and in ﴿law istaqamu﴾, and they agreed on the kasra in ﴿fa-qalu inna sami'na﴾, ﴿qul innama ad'u rabbi﴾, ﴿qul in adri﴾, and ﴿qul inni la amliku lakum﴾.

The "jadd" (majesty) according to the linguists is greatness and grandeur; one says "jadda fi 'aini," i.e., it became great in my eye. So the meaning: the greatness and majesty of our Lord is exalted. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid.

al-Hasan said: The intended meaning is His exalted wealth (ghina), and from this it is said of luck "jadd," and a man is "majdud," i.e., fortunate. In the hadith: "and wealth does not benefit the possessor of wealth (dha al-jadd) against You the wealth" — Abu 'Ubayd and al-Khalil said: i.e., wealth does not benefit the rich against You the riches; rather it is obedience that benefits him. Al-Qurtubi and al-Dahhak said: His jadd is His blessings and favors upon His creation.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: His dominion and authority.

al-Suddi said: His command.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding ﴿and that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾: i.e., exalted is our Lord. It has been said: His jadd is His power.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Allah has no jadd, and the jinn only said it out of ignorance.

The Jumhur read "jadd" with a fatha on the jim. 'Ikrimah, Abu Haywah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a kasra on the jim, which is the opposite of jest. Abu al-Ashhab read "jaddayi rabbina," i.e., its bounty and benefit.

It is also related from 'Ikrimah that he read with tanwin on "jaddun" and a raf' on "rabbuna," as a substitute (badal) for "jaddun."

﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾: this is an explanation of the exaltedness of His jadd, glory be to Him.

al-Zajjaj said: Exalted is the majesty and greatness of our Lord above taking a consort or a son. It seems the jinn, by this, alerted to the error of the disbelievers who attribute to Allah a consort and a son, and they declared Allah, glorified be He, free of both.

﴿And that the foolish one among us used to say about Allah an excessive lie (shatatan)﴾. The pronoun in "annahu" refers to the matter or the affair, and "safihuna" may be the subject of "kana," with "yaqulu" as the predicate; or "safihuna" may be the agent of "yaqulu," and the clause is the predicate of "kana," whose noun is a pronoun referring to the matter or the affair.

It is also permissible that "kana" be redundant (za'idah). By "their foolish one" they mean their disobedient ones and their polytheists.

Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Qatadah said: they meant by it Iblis. "Shatat" is excess in disbelief.

Abu Malik said: it is injustice (jawr). al-Kalbi said: it is lying. Its origin is deviation from the intended course and exceeding the limit.

From this is the poet's saying:
"In whatever condition they judged you, they went to excess, and that was only because the Wakhst directed you there."

﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never say a lie against Allah﴾, i.e., we reckoned that mankind and the jinn would not lie against Allah by claiming He has a partner, a consort and a son; therefore we believed them in that until we heard the Qur'an, and we knew the falsehood of their saying and the falsehood of what we used to suppose of them regarding truthfulness. The accusative of "kadhiban" is either a verbal noun emphasizing "yaqulu," since lying is a type of speech, or an adjective of a deleted verbal noun: i.e., "a lying speech."

Ya'qub, al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "an lan taqula" from "al-taqawwul," so that on this reading "kadhiban" is the direct object.

﴿And that there were men from mankind who used to seek refuge with men from the jinn﴾. al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: When an Arab man arrived at a valley, he would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people." So he would spend the night under his protection until morning, and this verse was revealed.

Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then from Banu Hanifah, then this spread among the Arabs; when Islam came, they sought refuge with Allah and abandoned them. ﴿So they increased them in rahaq﴾: i.e., the men of the jinn increased those who sought refuge with them from the men of mankind in rahaq, i.e., foolishness and transgression, i.e., arrogance and insolence; or those among mankind who sought refuge increased those they sought refuge with from the men of the jinn in rahaq, because those sought-refuge-with would say, "We have become lords over the jinn and mankind."

Mujahid and Qatadah said the first; Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said the second.

In the speech of the Arabs, "rahaq" means sin and the committing of forbidden things, and a man is "rahiq" if he is so; from this is His saying "tarhaquhum dhillatun" (humiliation will cover them), i.e., covers them. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:
"Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; does a lover find relief if he has not been struck by rahaq?"
meaning sin.

It has been said rahaq is fear, i.e., the jinn increased mankind in fear through this seeking of refuge with them. It has also been said that a man of mankind would say, "I seek refuge with so-and-so from the chiefs of the Arabs, from the jinn of this valley." This is supported by what has been said, that the word "rijal" is not applied to the jinn; so His saying "bi-rijalin" would be a description of those they seek refuge with from the men of mankind, i.e., they seek refuge with them from the evil of the jinn. This is far-fetched; and applying the word "rijal" to the jinn, even granting it is not linguistically correct, there is no barrier to applying it to them here by way of symmetry (mushakalah).

﴿And that they thought as you thought that Allah would never raise anyone﴾. This is from the speech of the jinn to mankind: i.e., and the jinn thought, as you, O mankind, thought, that there is no resurrection.

It has been said the meaning is: and mankind thought, as you, O jinn, thought, i.e., they do not believe in resurrection just as you do not believe.

﴿And that we touched the sky﴾. This is also from the speech of the jinn: i.e., we sought news, as our custom had been with it. ﴿Then we found it filled with a strong guard﴾ of angels guarding it against eavesdropping. "Harasan" is the plural of "haris" (guard), and "shadidan" is a description of "harasan": i.e., powerful; and "shuhuban" is the plural of "shihab," which is the flame drawn from the fire of a star, as its explanation was previously given in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We made them missiles for the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. The position of His saying "mulli'at harasan shadidan" is accusative, as the second object of "wajadna," since it is transitive to two objects; it is also permissible that it be transitive to one object, in which case the clause's position is accusative as a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, and "harasan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Its description with the singular is considered in terms of the wording, as one says "al-salaf al-salih," i.e., the righteous predecessors.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 72, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen﴾: that is, we, the company of the jinn, before this used to sit in the heavens on seats to listen, meaning places in which we sat to eavesdrop on news from the heavens. "Li-l-sam'" means seats existing for listening. "Maqā'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a noun of place. The rebellious jinn used to do this in order to hear news of the heavens from the angels and then convey it to the soothsayers (kahana). So God, exalted is He, guarded it by sending His Messenger (ﷺ) with flaming shooting stars. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿But whoever now listens will find a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾, that is, one is posted for him to be struck with it, or it is posted because of him to prevent him from listening. His words "al-'āna" (now) is a adverb of the present, and it is used figuratively for the future. The accusative of "rasadan" (lying in wait) is either as an attribute of "shihāban" (flame) or as an object of purpose. It is singular, but it may also be a collective noun like "al-haras" (the guard).

They have disagreed over whether the devils were struck with flames before the mission (al-mab'ath) or not. A group said: that did not happen.

Al-Wahidi related from Ma'mar, who said: I said to al-Zuhri: Were the stars thrown in the Jahiliyya? He said: Yes. I said: What do you think of His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in it﴾ and so on? He said: Its matter was made severe and intensified when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent.

Ibn Qutayba said: Stoning had occurred before his mission, but it was not like it in its severity of guarding after his mission. They used to steal some news in certain circumstances, but when he was sent they were prevented from that entirely.

'Abd al-Malik ibn Sabur said: The heavens were not guarded during the fatra (the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad). When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the heavens were guarded, the devils were struck with flames, and they were prevented from approaching the heaven.

Nafi' ibn Jubayr said: During the fatra, the devils used to listen and were not struck. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were struck with flames. The discussion of this has already preceded.

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾: that is, we do not know whether evil is intended for the people of the earth because of this guarding of the heaven, or whether their Lord intends for them rashad (guidance), that is, good.

Ibn Zayd said: Iblis said: We do not know whether God intended by this prevention to send down a punishment upon the people of the earth, or to send to them a messenger.

The word "sharrun" (evil) is in the nominative either by the construction of "ishtighāl" (the verb being occupied with the object, i.e., a verb governing a pronoun) or as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is what follows. The first is more preferable. The clause fills the place of the two objects of "nadri" (we know). The more appropriate view is that this is the speech of the jinn among themselves, not the speech of Iblis as Ibn Zayd said.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: that is, some said to others, when they called their companions to faith in Muhammad (ﷺ): We, before hearing the Qur'an, were among those described as righteous. ﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, a people below that, meaning below those described as righteous. It has been said that by "the righteous" he meant the believers, and by "those below that" the disbelievers. The first is more preferable.

The meaning of ﴿We were divided into different ways﴾ is: groups scattered apart and varied kinds. "Qidad" is the plural of "qidda," which is a piece of a thing. A people became "qidad" when their conditions became dispersed. From this is the poet's saying:

The one who holds back and extends, guiding to His obedience,
Amid the trials of people when their desires are scattered (qidad).
