**﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾**, meaning: I do not know whether the occurrence of the punishment you are promised is near. God, glorified be He, commanded him to say this to them in response to their saying to him: "When will this come about that you threaten us with?" 'Ata' said: He means that no one knows the Day of Resurrection except God alone. The meaning is that the knowledge of the time of the punishment is knowledge of the unseen, which no one knows except God.

The majority read *rabbi* (رَبِّي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. The two Harams (Makki and Madani) and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha.

In *man a'ada* (مَن أضْعَفُ), *man* is a relative pronoun, and *a'da'* (أضْعَفُ) is the predicate of an implied subject: meaning "he is weaker." The clause is the relative clause. It is also permissible for it to be interrogative, raised as a subject, with *a'da'* as its predicate, and the clause is in the position of an accusative filling the place of the two objects of *adri* (أدْرِي). His words *aqarib* (أقَرِيبٌ) are a fronted predicate, and *ma tu'adun* (ما تُوعَدُونَ) is a delayed subject.

**﴿Knower of the unseen﴾**: the majority read it in the nominative, as a substitute for *rabbi*, or an apposition to it, or the predicate of an implied subject, and the clause is a new sentence affirming what precedes it of lacking knowledge.

It has been read in the accusative as praise.

As-Sari read *'alima al-ghayb* (عَلِمَ الغَيْبَ) with a verbal form and the accusative of *al-ghayb*. The *fa'* in **﴿So He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾** indicates the sequence of non-disclosure upon His singular knowledge of the unseen, meaning: He does not inform anyone of the unseen, which is what is hidden from His servants.

Then He made an exception, saying: **﴿except whom He has approved of of the messengers﴾**, meaning: except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, or whom He has approved of among them, for disclosing to him some of His unseen, so that this would be a sign of his prophethood.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verses 14–28 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: When Allah (exalted is He) praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and reserved it for Himself to the exclusion of His creation, this is evidence that no one knows the unseen besides Him. Then He made an exception for whomever He approves of among the Messengers, so He entrusts them with whatever of His unseen He wills, by way of revelation to them. He makes this a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. The astrologer (munajjim) and whoever resembles him, from those who cast pebbles, read palms, and divine by mud, are not among the Messengers whom He approves and then informs of whatever He wills of His unseen. Such a person is a disbeliever in Allah, a fabricator against Him through his conjecture, his guesswork, and his lies.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" refers to Jibril (Gabriel). This interpretation is remote.

It has also been said that the meaning of "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" is that He informs him of some of His unseen, namely what relates to his mission, such as miracles, the rulings of obligations, the reward for deeds, and what He clarifies of the conditions of the Hereafter. It does not include unseen matters that do not relate to his mission, such as the time of the Hour and the like.

Al-Wahidi said: In this is evidence that whoever claims that the stars guide him to what will happen of events has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: In this is a refutation of miracles (karamat) of saints, because those who are attributed to them, even if they are approved saints, are not Messengers. Allah has specifically singled out the Messengers from among the approved ones with knowledge of the unseen. It is also a refutation of soothsaying (kihanah) and astrology (tanjim), because their practitioners are the furthest thing from being approved and the most deserving of wrath.

Al-Razi said: In my view, the verse contains no evidence for any of what they have said, since there is no general formula (sigha 'umum) in "His unseen." It is therefore restricted to one unseen matter, namely the time of the Resurrection, because it comes after His words: ﴿Is what you are promised near, or does my Lord set for it a distant term?﴾ (al-Jinn: 25).

If it is said: What then is the meaning of the exception in this case? We say: Perhaps when the Resurrection draws near He will make it manifest. And how could it not be so, when He said: ﴿On the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾ (al-Furqan: 25). Then the angels will know at that time the establishment of the Resurrection. Or the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: whomever He approves of among the Messengers, He places before him and behind him guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious jinn and humans.

What indicates that the intended meaning is not "He does not inform anyone of any of the unseen matters" is that it is established, in what approaches mass-transmission (mutawatir), that Shiqq and Satih were two soothsayers. They knew about the Prophet's ﷺ affair before his emergence, and they were famous for this knowledge among the Arabs, to the extent that Kisra (Khosrow) consulted them.

Thus it is established that Allah (exalted is He) may inform non-Messengers of some unseen matters. Also, the people of the religions (ahl al-milal) unanimously agree that the interpreter of dreams (mu'abbir al-ru'ya) reports future matters and is truthful in them. Also, Sultan Sanjar ibn Malik Shah transported a female soothsayer from Baghdad to Khurasan, asked her about future matters, and she informed him of them, and events happened in accordance with her words.

He said: People of verification (muhaqqiqun) in kalam and wisdom informed me that she reported unseen events in detail, and they occurred in accordance with her report.

Abu al-Barakat exaggerated in the book of ta'bir (interpretation) in describing her condition, and said: He investigated her condition for thirty years, and he verified that she used to report unseen matters with accurate correspondence.

Also, we witness this in people of true inspirations (ilhamat), and it is found among sorcerers as well. We also see astrological judgments matching, although they may differ. If we said that the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an, and the interpretation would be what we mentioned. End of his words.

I say: As for his statement that "there is no general formula in His unseen," it is false, because the annexation of a verbal noun (masdar) and a generic noun (ism jins) are among the formulas of generality, as the leading scholars of legal theory (usul) and others have stated.

As for his statement, "or the exception is disjunctive," it is a mere claim that the Qur'anic arrangement rejects.

As for his statement, "that Shiqq and Satih etc.," they lived in a time when the devils eavesdropped and passed what they heard to the soothsayers, so they mixed truth with falsehood, as established in the sound hadith.

In His saying ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ (al-Saffat: 10) and similar verses, and the matter of soothsaying has been explained in this Sharia, and that it was a path to some of the unseen through the devils' eavesdropping, until they were prevented from it by the Muhammadan mission.

They said: ﴿And we touched the sky, and found it filled with strong guards and flaming fires. And we used to sit in it on seats for listening, but whoever listens now finds a watching flame awaiting him﴾ (al-Jinn: 8–9). So the practice of soothsaying at the time it existed is specified by its own evidences, and it is among what this general statement is restricted by. Therefore, what he claims about the soothsaying's bearing on this verse is not a valid objection.

As for the story of the woman that he cited, it is a fable. Even if we grant the occurrence of some of the reports he narrated from her, it would be among what is in the hadith: "Among this community there are muhaddathun (those who are inspired), and among them is 'Umar." It would then be like a specification of the generality of this verse, not an implication of it. As for what he dared to say against Allah and His Book in the end of his statement, "if we said the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an," it is said to him: This is not your first slip, nor your first fall. How many similar and analogous things does the vein of your philosophy throb with, and the devil has spurred you so that he has you stumbling in the investigations of your tafsir! How strange you are! Would what reached you of the report of this woman and the like necessitate that criticism reach the Qur'an? How well said was the statement of one of the men of letters of our era:

"When the fly wishes to cover the sun, it spreads its wing over it."

And I said, among verses:

"A wind's path, it blocked it with a wing, and set a lamp against the light of dawn."

If you say: Then it has been established by this Qur'anic evidence that Allah reveals to whichever of His Messengers He approves whatever He wills of His unseen. Is it permissible for the Messenger to whom Allah revealed whatever He willed of His unseen to inform some of his community of it? I say: Yes, and there is no prohibition against that.

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of this what is not hidden from one knowledgeable in the pure Sunnah. Among that is what is sound: that he stood at a station (maqam) in which he informed of what would happen until the Day of Resurrection, and he left nothing that relates to trials (fitan) and the like unmentioned. Whoever memorized it memorized it, and whoever forgot it forgot it.

Likewise, what is established that Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman had been informed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the trials that would occur after him, to the extent that the senior Companions asked him about that and returned to him.

It is established in the Sahih and elsewhere that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked him about the trial that surges like the surging of the sea. He said: "Between you and it there is a door." 'Umar said: "Will it be opened or broken?" He said: "Rather, it will be broken." So 'Umar knew that the door was himself, and that breaking it meant killing him. As in the well-known sound hadith, it was said to Huzayfah: "Did 'Umar know that?" He said: "Yes, as he knows that tonight is before tomorrow."

Likewise, what is established of his informing Abu Dharr of what would happen to him, and his informing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib of the story of Dhu al-Thudayyah, and similar matters that are very numerous. If they were collected, a standalone compilation would result.

Given that this is established, there is no obstacle to some of the righteous (sulaha') of this community being specifically given some of the reports of the unseen that Allah manifested to His Messenger, and that His Messenger manifested to some of his community, and that this part of the community manifested to those after them. So the miracles (karamat) of the righteous are of this kind, and all of it is from the divine overflow (fayd rabbani) through the noble prophetic presence.

Then He (exalted is He) mentioned that He guards that unseen which the Messenger is informed of, and said: ﴿For He sends from before him and from behind him a guard﴾ (al-Jinn: 27). The sentence confirms the manifestation derived from the exception. The meaning is: He places before the Messenger and behind him a guard of angels who protect him from the devils' encroachment upon what He has manifested to him of the unseen. Or He places before the revelation and behind it a guard of angels who surround it so that the devils cannot steal it and convey it to the soothsayers. "All sides" is what is intended.

Al-Dahhak said: Allah did not send any prophet without angels with him who guard him from the devils, lest they take the form of an angel. If a devil came to him in the form of an angel, they would say: "This is a devil, so beware of him." And if the angel came, they would say: "This is the Messenger of your Lord."

Ibn Zayd said: "Rasadan" means guardians who guard the Prophet ﷺ from in front of him and behind him from the jinn and the devils.

Qatadah and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: They are four guardian angels.

Al-Farra' said: The intended one is Jibril.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "Rasad" is a group that watches like a guard, the singular, the plural, and the feminine are alike in this. "Rasad" for a thing is the one who observes it. It is said: "rasadahu, yarsuduhu, rasadan wa rasdan," and "tarassud" is watching for, and "marsad" is the place of watching.

﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. The lam is connected to "yaslukuh" (He sends). The intended meaning is knowledge connected to conveying that exists in actuality. The "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," its noun is the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence. "The messages" (risalat) refer to the unseen that Allah intended to manifest to whomever He approved of among the Messengers. The pronoun in "abla'u" (they have conveyed) refers to the guard.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: That Muhammad may know that the Messengers before him had conveyed the message, just as he conveyed the message. There is an omission to which the lam is connected: that is, We informed him of Our guarding of the revelation so that he would know that the Messengers before him were in his state of conveying.

It has been said: That Muhammad may know that Jibril and those with him had conveyed to him the messages of his Lord. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

It has been said: That the Messengers may know that the angels had conveyed the messages of their Lord.

It has been said: That Iblis may know that the Messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord without distortion.

Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, that the jinn may know that the Messengers had conveyed what was sent down to them, and that they were not the ones conveying it through the eavesdropping upon them.

Mujahid said: That whoever denied the Messengers may know that the Messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "liya'lama" with a fatha on the ya' (to know), in the active voice.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Hamid, Ya'qub, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a damma on it, in the passive voice: That people may know that the Messengers had conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: That Allah may know that His Messengers had conveyed His messages, meaning that He would know that by witnessing, just as He knew it as unseen.

Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam: ﴿and He has encompassed what is with them﴾, meaning, what is with the guard of angels, or what is with the conveying Messengers of His messages. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yaslukuh," with "qad" implied: that is, while He, exalted is He, has encompassed what is with them of conditions.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: That their Lord has encompassed what is with them, so they conveyed His messages. ﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾ of all things that were and that will be, and this is conjoined to "ahata" (He has encompassed).

"Adadan" may be in the accusative position as a specification (tamyiz) transferred from the object, meaning: He has counted the number of each thing, as in His saying: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ (al-Qamar: 12). It may also be in the accusative position as a verbal noun (masdar), or in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "counted." The meaning is that His (exalted is He) knowledge of things is not in a general manner but in a detailed manner, meaning: He has counted each individual of His creatures separately.

Ibn Jarir has reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Al-qasitun" are those who deviate (al-'adilun) from the truth.

Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning His words, ﴿If they had remained upright on the way﴾, that he said: "They maintained what they were commanded." ﴿We would have given them abundant water﴾: he said, "Flowing (ma'in)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi that he said: "ʿUmar said: ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water, that We might test them thereby﴾." He said: "Wherever there is water, there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth, there is temptation."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿that We might test them thereby﴾: he said, "That We might try them with it."

Concerning His words, ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment (ʿadhaban ṣaʿadan)﴾, he said: "A distance (shuqqah) of punishment in which he will be made to climb."

Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, reported from him concerning His words, ﴿He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾, that he said: "A mountain in Hell."

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, concerning ﴿a severe punishment﴾, that he said: "There is no respite in it."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning His words, ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah﴾, that he said: "On the day this verse was revealed, there was no mosque on earth except the Masjid al-Haram and the Masjid of Iliya' in Bayt al-Maqdis."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in ad-Dala'il reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out before the Hijrah to the outskirts of Makkah, and he drew a line for me and said: 'Do not do anything until I come to you.' Then he said: 'Let nothing you see frighten you.' So I advanced somewhat, then sat down, and there were black men like the men of the Zutt, and they were, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They nearly crowded around him in a mass (libadan)﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, who said: "When they heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting the Qur'an, they nearly mounted him out of eagerness for what they heard, and they drew close to him. He did not notice them until the messenger came to him, and he began to recite to him: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and adh-Dhiya' in al-Mukhtarah reported from him also, concerning the verse, that he said: "When the jinn came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying with his companions, bowing as he bowed and prostrating as he prostrated, they marvelled at the obedience of his companions, so they said to their people when the servant of Allah stood calling Him: ﴿They nearly crowded around him in a mass﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also, concerning ﴿when the servant of Allah stood calling Him﴾, that it means he was calling upon Allah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿they nearly crowded around him in a mass (libadan)﴾, that he said: "Helpers."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, concerning ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except whom He has approved of the messengers﴾, that he said: "Allah informs the Messenger of the unseen of revelation, and makes him aware of it from what has been revealed to him of His unseen and of what Allah decrees; no one else knows that."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, concerning ﴿a guard (rasadan)﴾, that he said: "They are successive angels who guard the Messenger of Allah from the devils until he conveys what he was sent with to them, and that is until the people of polytheism say: 'They have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, who said: "Allah did not send down any verse of the Qur'an to His Prophet without there being with it four angels who guard it until they deliver it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he recited: ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except whom He has approved of the messengers; for indeed He sends before him and behind him guards (rasadan)﴾, meaning the four angels, ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾." Ended.

**Its statement: ﴿And among us are the Muslims﴾** refers to those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). **﴿And among us are the unjust﴾**, meaning the oppressors and wrongdoers who swerved from the path of truth and inclined toward the path of falsehood. It is said *qasata* (قَسَطَ) when someone acted unjustly (*jara*), and *aqsata* (أَقْسَطَ) when someone acted justly (*adala*). **﴿Whoever submits, those have sought out a right course﴾**, meaning they aimed for the path of truth.

Al-Farra' (Abu Zakariyya al-Farra', the grammarian) said: they aimed for guidance (*al-huda*).

**﴿As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾**, meaning kindling for the Fire, which will be lit with them just as it is lit with the disbelievers among mankind.

**﴿And if they had remained upright on the way﴾**: this is not the speech of the jinn, but is coordinated with ﴿that it was [revealed to me that] a company of the jinn listened﴾. The meaning is: "It has been revealed to me that, had the jinn or mankind, or both, remained upright on the way, which is the way of Islam..." We have already mentioned that the reciters agreed on opening the *anna* (أنّ) here.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The opening here is based on an implied oath, whose interpretation is "By Allah, that if they had remained upright on the way..." Such usage occurs in speech, as in "By Allah, if you stood, I would stand," as in the words of the poet:

*"Indeed, by Allah, had you been free, and you are neither a free man nor a freed slave."*

He said: Or [*anna* is governed] by ﴿it was revealed to me that he listened﴾, [and] "if they had remained upright"; or by "we believed in it," meaning: we believed in it, and [we believed] that if they had remained upright...

The majority of reciters read the *waw* of *law* (لَوِ) with a kasra, due to the meeting of two unvocalised letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it with a damma: ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾, meaning abundant and plentiful.

Miqatil said: abundant water from the sky, after rain had been withheld from them for seven years.

Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is that if they had all believed, We would have expanded [their provision] for them in this world. Abundant water is cited as a parable, because all good and provision come by rain. This is like His words: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 65], and His words: ﴿Whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3], and His words: ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving; He will send the sky upon you in abundance, and will increase you in wealth and children﴾ [Nuh: 10–12], and so on.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "And that if their father had remained upright in his worship, and prostrated to Adam, and had not disbelieved, and his offspring had followed him in Islam, We would have bestowed favours upon them." Al-Zajjaj chose this view.

*Al-ma' al-ghadaq* (الماء الغَدَق) is the abundant water in the language of the Arabs.

**﴿So that We may test them therein﴾**, meaning so that We may try them and know how they would give thanks for those blessings.

Al-Kalbi said: The meaning is: "And that if they had remained upright on the way they were on, of disbelief, and they had all been disbelievers, We would have expanded their provisions as a scheme against them and a gradual leading-on, until they are tried thereby, and We punish them in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Thumali, Yaman ibn Zayyan, Ibn Kaysan, and Abu Mijlaz said the same, and they cited His words: ﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and His words: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one nation, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33], and so on. But the first view is preferable.

**﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾**, meaning: whoever turns away from the Qur'an, or from worship, or from admonition, or from all of that, He will make him enter, [that is,] a punishment of *sa'ad* (صَعَدًا), meaning arduous and difficult.

The majority read *naslukuhu* (نَسْلُكْهُ) with an open *nun*. The Kufans and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read it with a *ya'* (يَ), and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading, because of His words ﴿from the remembrance of his Lord﴾, and He did not say "from Our remembrance."

Muslim ibn Jundub, Talha ibn Musarrif, and al-A'raj read it with a damma on the *nun* and a kasra on the *lam*, from *aslakahu* (أَسْلَكَهُ), whereas the majority read it from *salakahu* (سَلَكَهُ).

*Al-sa'ad* (الصَّعَدُ) in the language means hardship. One says *tasa''ada bi al-amr* (تَصَعَّدَ بِي الأمْرُ) when a matter becomes difficult for you. It is a verbal noun from *sa'ida* (صَعِدَ), one says *sa'ida sa'dan wa su'udan* (صَعِدَ صَعْدًا وصُعُودًا). It is applied to the punishment as an intensification, because it climbs over the one being punished, meaning it overtakes and overpowers him so that he cannot bear it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-sa'ad* is a verbal noun, meaning a punishment having *sa'ad*.

'Ikrima said: *al-sa'ad* is a smooth rock in Hell, which the disbeliever is charged to climb. When he reaches its top, he is cast down into Hell, as in His words: ﴿I will drive him to a steep climb﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17]. *Al-su'ud* (الصَّعُودُ) is a difficult ascent.

**﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾**: we have already mentioned the agreement of the reciters here upon the opening (*fath*) [of *anna*]. It is coordinated with *annahu istama'a* (أَنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ), meaning: "and it has been revealed to me that the mosques are exclusively for God."

Al-Khalil said: the implied construction is *wa li-anna al-masajid* (وَلِأنَّ المَساجِدَ), "and because the mosques..."

*Al-masajid* (المَساجِدُ) are the places built for prayer therein.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The jinn said, "How can we come to the mosques and witness the prayer with you, when we are far from you?" So this was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: By it He means every place, for the whole earth is a mosque.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Talq ibn Habib said: By the mosques He means the limbs upon which the servant prostrates, which are the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, and the forehead. [They explained:] "These are limbs with which God has blessed you, so do not prostrate with them to other than Him, lest you deny the blessing of God." 'Ata' also said this.

It has been said that *al-masajid* is the prayer, because prostration is one of its pillars. This was said by al-Hasan.

**﴿So do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾** from among His creation, whoever it may be.

**﴿And that when the servant of God stood up﴾**: we have already mentioned that the majority read *anna* here with an opening, coordinated with ﴿that he listened﴾, meaning: "and it has been revealed to me that when the servant of God, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), stood up calling upon Him," meaning calling upon God and worshipping Him. This was in the valley of Nakhlah, as has been mentioned earlier, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood praying and reciting the Qur'an. We have also already mentioned the reading of the one who read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra here, and in it there is obscurity and remoteness from the intended meaning.

**﴿They almost became a mass upon him﴾**, meaning the jinn almost became a mass (*libadan*, لِبَدًا) upon the Messenger of God, i.e., massed together from their crowding upon him to listen to the Qur'an from him.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of *libadan* is that some ride upon others. From this derives the word for the felt rugs (*lubud*, لُبُودِ) that are spread out.

The majority read *libadan* with a kasra on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'*. Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham read it with a damma on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'*. Abu Hayawa, Muhammad ibn al-Samayfa', al-Uqayli, and al-Jahdari read it with a damma on both the *ba'* and the *lam*. Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-A'raj read it with a damma on the *lam* and a shadda on the *ba'*, with a fatha.

According to the first reading, the meaning is what we have mentioned. According to the reading with a damma on the *lam*, the meaning is "many," as in His words: ﴿I have squandered wealth in abundance﴾ [al-Balad: 6]. It has also been said that the meaning is: the polytheists almost rode upon one another out of rage against the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd said: When the servant of God, Muhammad, stood up with the call, mankind and the jinn massed together against this matter in order to extinguish it, but God refused except that He should give him victory and perfect His light.

Ibn Jarir chose this view.

Mujahid said: *libadan* means groups, from *talabbada al-shay' 'ala al-shay'* (تَلَبَّدَ الشَّيْءُ عَلى الشَّيْءِ), meaning it gathered together upon something. From it comes *al-labad* (اللَّبَدُ), which is spread out, because its wool is piled up. Anything you stick firmly to something else is said to be *labbadtahu* (لَبَّدْتَهُ). The hair on a lion's back is called *lubdah* (لُبْدَةٌ), and its plural is *lubad*. Large swarms of locusts are also called *lubad*. *Al-lubad* with a damma on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'* is applied to something lasting, and from this it was said that the vulture of Luqman is called *Lubad*, because of its long life. This is what is meant by the words of al-Nabighah:

*"The one who wore down upon her wore down upon Lubad."*

**﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾**, meaning: the servant of God said, "I only call upon my Lord and worship Him, **and I associate no one with Him**" from His creation.

The majority read *qala* (قالَ, "he said"). 'Asim and Hamza read *qul* (قُلْ, "say") as an imperative.

The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You have brought a grave matter, and you have antagonised all the people. Turn back from this, and we will protect you."

**﴿Say: I possess for you neither harm nor right guidance﴾**, meaning: I am not able to repel harm from you, nor to bring good to you. It has been said that *al-durr* (الضُّرُّ) is disbelief and *al-rashad* (الرَّشَدُ) is guidance. The first view is preferable, because the two indefinite nouns occur in a context of negation, so they encompass every harm and every right guidance, in this world and in religion.

**﴿Say: No one will protect me from God, nor will I find besides Him any refuge﴾**, meaning: no one can ward off His punishment from me if He sends it upon me. *Multahadan* (مُلْتَحَدًا) means a place of refuge, a place to turn to, and a shelter. Al-Kalbi said: a place of entry into the earth, like a burrow. It has been said: a way and a path. The meanings are close, and from it is the poet's saying:

*"Alas for my soul, and alas that it is useless for me, and there is no refuge from God's decree."*

The exception in His words **﴿except a message from God﴾** is related to His words *la amliku* (لا أمْلِكُ, "I possess not"): meaning, "I possess neither harm nor right guidance, except the conveyance from God, for in it is the greatest right guidance," or it is related to *multahadan*, meaning: "I will not find besides Him any refuge, except the conveyance."

Miqatil said: That is what protects me from His punishment.

Qatada said: **﴿except a message from God﴾**: that is what I possess by God's grace. As for disbelief and faith, I do not possess them.

Al-Farra' said: "But I convey to you what I have been sent with." On this view it is an exception of separation (*munqati'*).

Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative as a substitute for *multahadan*, meaning: "and I will not find besides Him any refuge, except that I convey what comes from God." His words **"and His messages"** are coordinated with *balaghan* (بَلاغًا), meaning: "except a message from God and His messages that He sent me with to you." Or: "except that I convey from God and act upon His messages, so that I hold myself to what I command others." It has also been said: *al-risalat* (الرِّسالاتُ) is coordinated with the noble noun (*al-ism al-sharif*), meaning: "except a message from God and from His messages." Abu Hayyan said this and preferred it.

**﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger﴾** in the command to monotheism, because the context concerns it, **﴿then indeed for him is the Fire of Hell﴾**. The majority read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra, as an independent new sentence.

It has been read with a fatha on the hamza, because what follows the *fa'* of the apodosis is in the position of a new beginning, and the implied construction is *fa-jaza'uhu anna lahu nara jahannam* (فَجَزاؤُهُ أنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ), "so his recompense is that for him is the Fire of Hell," or *fa-hukmuhu anna lahu nara jahannam* (فَحُكْمُهُ أنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ), "so his judgement is that for him is the Fire of Hell."

*Khalidina fiha* (خالِدِينَ فِيها) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: "in the Fire" or "in Hell." The plural is according to the meaning of *man* (مَن), just as the singular in His words *fa-inna lahu* (فَإنَّ لَهُ) is according to its wording. His words **"forever" (abadan)** are an emphasis of the meaning of eternal abiding, meaning: abiding therein without end.

**﴿Until, when they see what they are promised﴾**, meaning the punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter.

The meaning is: they will not cease in their state of persistence in disbelief and enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, **until, when they see what they are promised**, **﴿they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾**, meaning: who is weaker in army, by which he would be given victory, and fewer in number: they or the believers?

**﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾**, meaning: I do not know whether the occurrence of the punishment you are promised is near. God, glorified be He, commanded him to say this to them in response to their saying to him: "When will this come about that you threaten us with?" 'Ata' said: He means that no one knows the Day of Resurrection except God alone. The meaning is that the knowledge of the time of the punishment is knowledge of the unseen, which no one knows except God.

The majority read *rabbi* (رَبِّي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. The two Harams (Makki and Madani) and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha.

In *man a'ada* (مَن أضْعَفُ), *man* is a relative pronoun, and *a'da'* (أضْعَفُ) is the predicate of an implied subject: meaning "he is weaker." The clause is the relative clause. It is also permissible for it to be interrogative, raised as a subject, with *a'da'* as its predicate, and the clause is in the position of an accusative filling the place of the two objects of *adri* (أدْرِي). His words *aqarib* (أقَرِيبٌ) are a fronted predicate, and *ma tu'adun* (ما تُوعَدُونَ) is a delayed subject.

**﴿Knower of the unseen﴾**: the majority read it in the nominative, as a substitute for *rabbi*, or an apposition to it, or the predicate of an implied subject, and the clause is a new sentence affirming what precedes it of lacking knowledge.

It has been read in the accusative as praise.

As-Sari read *'alima al-ghayb* (عَلِمَ الغَيْبَ) with a verbal form and the accusative of *al-ghayb*. The *fa'* in **﴿So He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾** indicates the sequence of non-disclosure upon His singular knowledge of the unseen, meaning: He does not inform anyone of the unseen, which is what is hidden from His servants.

Then He made an exception, saying: **﴿except whom He has approved of of the messengers﴾**, meaning: except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, or whom He has approved of among them, for disclosing to him some of His unseen, so that this would be a sign of his prophethood.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verses 14–28 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: When Allah (exalted is He) praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and reserved it for Himself to the exclusion of His creation, this is evidence that no one knows the unseen besides Him. Then He made an exception for whomever He approves of among the Messengers, so He entrusts them with whatever of His unseen He wills, by way of revelation to them. He makes this a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. The astrologer (munajjim) and whoever resembles him, from those who cast pebbles, read palms, and divine by mud, are not among the Messengers whom He approves and then informs of whatever He wills of His unseen. Such a person is a disbeliever in Allah, a fabricator against Him through his conjecture, his guesswork, and his lies.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" refers to Jibril (Gabriel). This interpretation is remote.

It has also been said that the meaning of "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" is that He informs him of some of His unseen, namely what relates to his mission, such as miracles, the rulings of obligations, the reward for deeds, and what He clarifies of the conditions of the Hereafter. It does not include unseen matters that do not relate to his mission, such as the time of the Hour and the like.

Al-Wahidi said: In this is evidence that whoever claims that the stars guide him to what will happen of events has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: In this is a refutation of miracles (karamat) of saints, because those who are attributed to them, even if they are approved saints, are not Messengers. Allah has specifically singled out the Messengers from among the approved ones with knowledge of the unseen. It is also a refutation of soothsaying (kihanah) and astrology (tanjim), because their practitioners are the furthest thing from being approved and the most deserving of wrath.

Al-Razi said: In my view, the verse contains no evidence for any of what they have said, since there is no general formula (sigha 'umum) in "His unseen." It is therefore restricted to one unseen matter, namely the time of the Resurrection, because it comes after His words: ﴿Is what you are promised near, or does my Lord set for it a distant term?﴾ (al-Jinn: 25).

If it is said: What then is the meaning of the exception in this case? We say: Perhaps when the Resurrection draws near He will make it manifest. And how could it not be so, when He said: ﴿On the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾ (al-Furqan: 25). Then the angels will know at that time the establishment of the Resurrection. Or the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: whomever He approves of among the Messengers, He places before him and behind him guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious jinn and humans.

What indicates that the intended meaning is not "He does not inform anyone of any of the unseen matters" is that it is established, in what approaches mass-transmission (mutawatir), that Shiqq and Satih were two soothsayers. They knew about the Prophet's ﷺ affair before his emergence, and they were famous for this knowledge among the Arabs, to the extent that Kisra (Khosrow) consulted them.

Thus it is established that Allah (exalted is He) may inform non-Messengers of some unseen matters. Also, the people of the religions (ahl al-milal) unanimously agree that the interpreter of dreams (mu'abbir al-ru'ya) reports future matters and is truthful in them. Also, Sultan Sanjar ibn Malik Shah transported a female soothsayer from Baghdad to Khurasan, asked her about future matters, and she informed him of them, and events happened in accordance with her words.

He said: People of verification (muhaqqiqun) in kalam and wisdom informed me that she reported unseen events in detail, and they occurred in accordance with her report.

Abu al-Barakat exaggerated in the book of ta'bir (interpretation) in describing her condition, and said: He investigated her condition for thirty years, and he verified that she used to report unseen matters with accurate correspondence.

Also, we witness this in people of true inspirations (ilhamat), and it is found among sorcerers as well. We also see astrological judgments matching, although they may differ. If we said that the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an, and the interpretation would be what we mentioned. End of his words.

I say: As for his statement that "there is no general formula in His unseen," it is false, because the annexation of a verbal noun (masdar) and a generic noun (ism jins) are among the formulas of generality, as the leading scholars of legal theory (usul) and others have stated.

As for his statement, "or the exception is disjunctive," it is a mere claim that the Qur'anic arrangement rejects.

As for his statement, "that Shiqq and Satih etc.," they lived in a time when the devils eavesdropped and passed what they heard to the soothsayers, so they mixed truth with falsehood, as established in the sound hadith.

In His saying ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ (al-Saffat: 10) and similar verses, and the matter of soothsaying has been explained in this Sharia, and that it was a path to some of the unseen through the devils' eavesdropping, until they were prevented from it by the Muhammadan mission.

They said: ﴿And we touched the sky, and found it filled with strong guards and flaming fires. And we used to sit in it on seats for listening, but whoever listens now finds a watching flame awaiting him﴾ (al-Jinn: 8–9). So the practice of soothsaying at the time it existed is specified by its own evidences, and it is among what this general statement is restricted by. Therefore, what he claims about the soothsaying's bearing on this verse is not a valid objection.

As for the story of the woman that he cited, it is a fable. Even if we grant the occurrence of some of the reports he narrated from her, it would be among what is in the hadith: "Among this community there are muhaddathun (those who are inspired), and among them is 'Umar." It would then be like a specification of the generality of this verse, not an implication of it. As for what he dared to say against Allah and His Book in the end of his statement, "if we said the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an," it is said to him: This is not your first slip, nor your first fall. How many similar and analogous things does the vein of your philosophy throb with, and the devil has spurred you so that he has you stumbling in the investigations of your tafsir! How strange you are! Would what reached you of the report of this woman and the like necessitate that criticism reach the Qur'an? How well said was the statement of one of the men of letters of our era:

"When the fly wishes to cover the sun, it spreads its wing over it."

And I said, among verses:

"A wind's path, it blocked it with a wing, and set a lamp against the light of dawn."

If you say: Then it has been established by this Qur'anic evidence that Allah reveals to whichever of His Messengers He approves whatever He wills of His unseen. Is it permissible for the Messenger to whom Allah revealed whatever He willed of His unseen to inform some of his community of it? I say: Yes, and there is no prohibition against that.

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of this what is not hidden from one knowledgeable in the pure Sunnah. Among that is what is sound: that he stood at a station (maqam) in which he informed of what would happen until the Day of Resurrection, and he left nothing that relates to trials (fitan) and the like unmentioned. Whoever memorized it memorized it, and whoever forgot it forgot it.

Likewise, what is established that Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman had been informed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the trials that would occur after him, to the extent that the senior Companions asked him about that and returned to him.

It is established in the Sahih and elsewhere that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked him about the trial that surges like the surging of the sea. He said: "Between you and it there is a door." 'Umar said: "Will it be opened or broken?" He said: "Rather, it will be broken." So 'Umar knew that the door was himself, and that breaking it meant killing him. As in the well-known sound hadith, it was said to Huzayfah: "Did 'Umar know that?" He said: "Yes, as he knows that tonight is before tomorrow."

Likewise, what is established of his informing Abu Dharr of what would happen to him, and his informing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib of the story of Dhu al-Thudayyah, and similar matters that are very numerous. If they were collected, a standalone compilation would result.

Given that this is established, there is no obstacle to some of the righteous (sulaha') of this community being specifically given some of the reports of the unseen that Allah manifested to His Messenger, and that His Messenger manifested to some of his community, and that this part of the community manifested to those after them. So the miracles (karamat) of the righteous are of this kind, and all of it is from the divine overflow (fayd rabbani) through the noble prophetic presence.

Then He (exalted is He) mentioned that He guards that unseen which the Messenger is informed of, and said: ﴿For He sends from before him and from behind him a guard﴾ (al-Jinn: 27). The sentence confirms the manifestation derived from the exception. The meaning is: He places before the Messenger and behind him a guard of angels who protect him from the devils' encroachment upon what He has manifested to him of the unseen. Or He places before the revelation and behind it a guard of angels who surround it so that the devils cannot steal it and convey it to the soothsayers. "All sides" is what is intended.

Al-Dahhak said: Allah did not send any prophet without angels with him who guard him from the devils, lest they take the form of an angel. If a devil came to him in the form of an angel, they would say: "This is a devil, so beware of him." And if the angel came, they would say: "This is the Messenger of your Lord."

Ibn Zayd said: "Rasadan" means guardians who guard the Prophet ﷺ from in front of him and behind him from the jinn and the devils.

Qatadah and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: They are four guardian angels.

Al-Farra' said: The intended one is Jibril.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "Rasad" is a group that watches like a guard, the singular, the plural, and the feminine are alike in this. "Rasad" for a thing is the one who observes it. It is said: "rasadahu, yarsuduhu, rasadan wa rasdan," and "tarassud" is watching for, and "marsad" is the place of watching.

﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. The lam is connected to "yaslukuh" (He sends). The intended meaning is knowledge connected to conveying that exists in actuality. The "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," its noun is the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence. "The messages" (risalat) refer to the unseen that Allah intended to manifest to whomever He approved of among the Messengers. The pronoun in "abla'u" (they have conveyed) refers to the guard.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: That Muhammad may know that the Messengers before him had conveyed the message, just as he conveyed the message. There is an omission to which the lam is connected: that is, We informed him of Our guarding of the revelation so that he would know that the Messengers before him were in his state of conveying.

It has been said: That Muhammad may know that Jibril and those with him had conveyed to him the messages of his Lord. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

It has been said: That the Messengers may know that the angels had conveyed the messages of their Lord.

It has been said: That Iblis may know that the Messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord without distortion.

Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, that the jinn may know that the Messengers had conveyed what was sent down to them, and that they were not the ones conveying it through the eavesdropping upon them.

Mujahid said: That whoever denied the Messengers may know that the Messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "liya'lama" with a fatha on the ya' (to know), in the active voice.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Hamid, Ya'qub, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a damma on it, in the passive voice: That people may know that the Messengers had conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: That Allah may know that His Messengers had conveyed His messages, meaning that He would know that by witnessing, just as He knew it as unseen.

Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam: ﴿and He has encompassed what is with them﴾, meaning, what is with the guard of angels, or what is with the conveying Messengers of His messages. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yaslukuh," with "qad" implied: that is, while He, exalted is He, has encompassed what is with them of conditions.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: That their Lord has encompassed what is with them, so they conveyed His messages. ﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾ of all things that were and that will be, and this is conjoined to "ahata" (He has encompassed).

"Adadan" may be in the accusative position as a specification (tamyiz) transferred from the object, meaning: He has counted the number of each thing, as in His saying: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ (al-Qamar: 12). It may also be in the accusative position as a verbal noun (masdar), or in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "counted." The meaning is that His (exalted is He) knowledge of things is not in a general manner but in a detailed manner, meaning: He has counted each individual of His creatures separately.

Ibn Jarir has reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Al-qasitun" are those who deviate (al-'adilun) from the truth.

Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning His words, ﴿If they had remained upright on the way﴾, that he said: "They maintained what they were commanded." ﴿We would have given them abundant water﴾: he said, "Flowing (ma'in)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi that he said: "ʿUmar said: ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water, that We might test them thereby﴾." He said: "Wherever there is water, there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth, there is temptation."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿that We might test them thereby﴾: he said, "That We might try them with it."

Concerning His words, ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment (ʿadhaban ṣaʿadan)﴾, he said: "A distance (shuqqah) of punishment in which he will be made to climb."

Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, reported from him concerning His words, ﴿He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾, that he said: "A mountain in Hell."

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, concerning ﴿a severe punishment﴾, that he said: "There is no respite in it."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning His words, ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah﴾, that he said: "On the day this verse was revealed, there was no mosque on earth except the Masjid al-Haram and the Masjid of Iliya' in Bayt al-Maqdis."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in ad-Dala'il reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out before the Hijrah to the outskirts of Makkah, and he drew a line for me and said: 'Do not do anything until I come to you.' Then he said: 'Let nothing you see frighten you.' So I advanced somewhat, then sat down, and there were black men like the men of the Zutt, and they were, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They nearly crowded around him in a mass (libadan)﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, who said: "When they heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting the Qur'an, they nearly mounted him out of eagerness for what they heard, and they drew close to him. He did not notice them until the messenger came to him, and he began to recite to him: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and adh-Dhiya' in al-Mukhtarah reported from him also, concerning the verse, that he said: "When the jinn came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying with his companions, bowing as he bowed and prostrating as he prostrated, they marvelled at the obedience of his companions, so they said to their people when the servant of Allah stood calling Him: ﴿They nearly crowded around him in a mass﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also, concerning ﴿when the servant of Allah stood calling Him﴾, that it means he was calling upon Allah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿they nearly crowded around him in a mass (libadan)﴾, that he said: "Helpers."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, concerning ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except whom He has approved of the messengers﴾, that he said: "Allah informs the Messenger of the unseen of revelation, and makes him aware of it from what has been revealed to him of His unseen and of what Allah decrees; no one else knows that."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, concerning ﴿a guard (rasadan)﴾, that he said: "They are successive angels who guard the Messenger of Allah from the devils until he conveys what he was sent with to them, and that is until the people of polytheism say: 'They have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also, who said: "Allah did not send down any verse of the Qur'an to His Prophet without there being with it four angels who guard it until they deliver it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he recited: ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except whom He has approved of the messengers; for indeed He sends before him and behind him guards (rasadan)﴾, meaning the four angels, ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾." Ended.

**Its statement: ﴿And among us are the Muslims﴾** refers to those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). **﴿And among us are the unjust﴾**, meaning the oppressors and wrongdoers who swerved from the path of truth and inclined toward the path of falsehood. It is said *qasata* (قَسَطَ) when someone acted unjustly (*jara*), and *aqsata* (أَقْسَطَ) when someone acted justly (*adala*). **﴿Whoever submits, those have sought out a right course﴾**, meaning they aimed for the path of truth.

Al-Farra' (Abu Zakariyya al-Farra', the grammarian) said: they aimed for guidance (*al-huda*).

**﴿As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾**, meaning kindling for the Fire, which will be lit with them just as it is lit with the disbelievers among mankind.

**﴿And if they had remained upright on the way﴾**: this is not the speech of the jinn, but is coordinated with ﴿that it was [revealed to me that] a company of the jinn listened﴾. The meaning is: "It has been revealed to me that, had the jinn or mankind, or both, remained upright on the way, which is the way of Islam..." We have already mentioned that the reciters agreed on opening the *anna* (أنّ) here.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The opening here is based on an implied oath, whose interpretation is "By Allah, that if they had remained upright on the way..." Such usage occurs in speech, as in "By Allah, if you stood, I would stand," as in the words of the poet:

*"Indeed, by Allah, had you been free, and you are neither a free man nor a freed slave."*

He said: Or [*anna* is governed] by ﴿it was revealed to me that he listened﴾, [and] "if they had remained upright"; or by "we believed in it," meaning: we believed in it, and [we believed] that if they had remained upright...

The majority of reciters read the *waw* of *law* (لَوِ) with a kasra, due to the meeting of two unvocalised letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it with a damma: ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾, meaning abundant and plentiful.

Miqatil said: abundant water from the sky, after rain had been withheld from them for seven years.

Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is that if they had all believed, We would have expanded [their provision] for them in this world. Abundant water is cited as a parable, because all good and provision come by rain. This is like His words: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 65], and His words: ﴿Whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3], and His words: ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving; He will send the sky upon you in abundance, and will increase you in wealth and children﴾ [Nuh: 10–12], and so on.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "And that if their father had remained upright in his worship, and prostrated to Adam, and had not disbelieved, and his offspring had followed him in Islam, We would have bestowed favours upon them." Al-Zajjaj chose this view.

*Al-ma' al-ghadaq* (الماء الغَدَق) is the abundant water in the language of the Arabs.

**﴿So that We may test them therein﴾**, meaning so that We may try them and know how they would give thanks for those blessings.

Al-Kalbi said: The meaning is: "And that if they had remained upright on the way they were on, of disbelief, and they had all been disbelievers, We would have expanded their provisions as a scheme against them and a gradual leading-on, until they are tried thereby, and We punish them in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Thumali, Yaman ibn Zayyan, Ibn Kaysan, and Abu Mijlaz said the same, and they cited His words: ﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and His words: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one nation, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33], and so on. But the first view is preferable.

**﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾**, meaning: whoever turns away from the Qur'an, or from worship, or from admonition, or from all of that, He will make him enter, [that is,] a punishment of *sa'ad* (صَعَدًا), meaning arduous and difficult.

The majority read *naslukuhu* (نَسْلُكْهُ) with an open *nun*. The Kufans and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read it with a *ya'* (يَ), and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading, because of His words ﴿from the remembrance of his Lord﴾, and He did not say "from Our remembrance."

Muslim ibn Jundub, Talha ibn Musarrif, and al-A'raj read it with a damma on the *nun* and a kasra on the *lam*, from *aslakahu* (أَسْلَكَهُ), whereas the majority read it from *salakahu* (سَلَكَهُ).

*Al-sa'ad* (الصَّعَدُ) in the language means hardship. One says *tasa''ada bi al-amr* (تَصَعَّدَ بِي الأمْرُ) when a matter becomes difficult for you. It is a verbal noun from *sa'ida* (صَعِدَ), one says *sa'ida sa'dan wa su'udan* (صَعِدَ صَعْدًا وصُعُودًا). It is applied to the punishment as an intensification, because it climbs over the one being punished, meaning it overtakes and overpowers him so that he cannot bear it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-sa'ad* is a verbal noun, meaning a punishment having *sa'ad*.

'Ikrima said: *al-sa'ad* is a smooth rock in Hell, which the disbeliever is charged to climb. When he reaches its top, he is cast down into Hell, as in His words: ﴿I will drive him to a steep climb﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17]. *Al-su'ud* (الصَّعُودُ) is a difficult ascent.

**﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾**: we have already mentioned the agreement of the reciters here upon the opening (*fath*) [of *anna*]. It is coordinated with *annahu istama'a* (أَنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ), meaning: "and it has been revealed to me that the mosques are exclusively for God."

Al-Khalil said: the implied construction is *wa li-anna al-masajid* (وَلِأنَّ المَساجِدَ), "and because the mosques..."

*Al-masajid* (المَساجِدُ) are the places built for prayer therein.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The jinn said, "How can we come to the mosques and witness the prayer with you, when we are far from you?" So this was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: By it He means every place, for the whole earth is a mosque.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Talq ibn Habib said: By the mosques He means the limbs upon which the servant prostrates, which are the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, and the forehead. [They explained:] "These are limbs with which God has blessed you, so do not prostrate with them to other than Him, lest you deny the blessing of God." 'Ata' also said this.

It has been said that *al-masajid* is the prayer, because prostration is one of its pillars. This was said by al-Hasan.

**﴿So do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾** from among His creation, whoever it may be.

**﴿And that when the servant of God stood up﴾**: we have already mentioned that the majority read *anna* here with an opening, coordinated with ﴿that he listened﴾, meaning: "and it has been revealed to me that when the servant of God, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), stood up calling upon Him," meaning calling upon God and worshipping Him. This was in the valley of Nakhlah, as has been mentioned earlier, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood praying and reciting the Qur'an. We have also already mentioned the reading of the one who read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra here, and in it there is obscurity and remoteness from the intended meaning.

**﴿They almost became a mass upon him﴾**, meaning the jinn almost became a mass (*libadan*, لِبَدًا) upon the Messenger of God, i.e., massed together from their crowding upon him to listen to the Qur'an from him.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of *libadan* is that some ride upon others. From this derives the word for the felt rugs (*lubud*, لُبُودِ) that are spread out.

The majority read *libadan* with a kasra on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'*. Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham read it with a damma on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'*. Abu Hayawa, Muhammad ibn al-Samayfa', al-Uqayli, and al-Jahdari read it with a damma on both the *ba'* and the *lam*. Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-A'raj read it with a damma on the *lam* and a shadda on the *ba'*, with a fatha.

According to the first reading, the meaning is what we have mentioned. According to the reading with a damma on the *lam*, the meaning is "many," as in His words: ﴿I have squandered wealth in abundance﴾ [al-Balad: 6]. It has also been said that the meaning is: the polytheists almost rode upon one another out of rage against the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd said: When the servant of God, Muhammad, stood up with the call, mankind and the jinn massed together against this matter in order to extinguish it, but God refused except that He should give him victory and perfect His light.

Ibn Jarir chose this view.

Mujahid said: *libadan* means groups, from *talabbada al-shay' 'ala al-shay'* (تَلَبَّدَ الشَّيْءُ عَلى الشَّيْءِ), meaning it gathered together upon something. From it comes *al-labad* (اللَّبَدُ), which is spread out, because its wool is piled up. Anything you stick firmly to something else is said to be *labbadtahu* (لَبَّدْتَهُ). The hair on a lion's back is called *lubdah* (لُبْدَةٌ), and its plural is *lubad*. Large swarms of locusts are also called *lubad*. *Al-lubad* with a damma on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ba'* is applied to something lasting, and from this it was said that the vulture of Luqman is called *Lubad*, because of its long life. This is what is meant by the words of al-Nabighah:

*"The one who wore down upon her wore down upon Lubad."*

**﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾**, meaning: the servant of God said, "I only call upon my Lord and worship Him, **and I associate no one with Him**" from His creation.

The majority read *qala* (قالَ, "he said"). 'Asim and Hamza read *qul* (قُلْ, "say") as an imperative.

The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You have brought a grave matter, and you have antagonised all the people. Turn back from this, and we will protect you."

**﴿Say: I possess for you neither harm nor right guidance﴾**, meaning: I am not able to repel harm from you, nor to bring good to you. It has been said that *al-durr* (الضُّرُّ) is disbelief and *al-rashad* (الرَّشَدُ) is guidance. The first view is preferable, because the two indefinite nouns occur in a context of negation, so they encompass every harm and every right guidance, in this world and in religion.

**﴿Say: No one will protect me from God, nor will I find besides Him any refuge﴾**, meaning: no one can ward off His punishment from me if He sends it upon me. *Multahadan* (مُلْتَحَدًا) means a place of refuge, a place to turn to, and a shelter. Al-Kalbi said: a place of entry into the earth, like a burrow. It has been said: a way and a path. The meanings are close, and from it is the poet's saying:

*"Alas for my soul, and alas that it is useless for me, and there is no refuge from God's decree."*

The exception in His words **﴿except a message from God﴾** is related to His words *la amliku* (لا أمْلِكُ, "I possess not"): meaning, "I possess neither harm nor right guidance, except the conveyance from God, for in it is the greatest right guidance," or it is related to *multahadan*, meaning: "I will not find besides Him any refuge, except the conveyance."

Miqatil said: That is what protects me from His punishment.

Qatada said: **﴿except a message from God﴾**: that is what I possess by God's grace. As for disbelief and faith, I do not possess them.

Al-Farra' said: "But I convey to you what I have been sent with." On this view it is an exception of separation (*munqati'*).

Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative as a substitute for *multahadan*, meaning: "and I will not find besides Him any refuge, except that I convey what comes from God." His words **"and His messages"** are coordinated with *balaghan* (بَلاغًا), meaning: "except a message from God and His messages that He sent me with to you." Or: "except that I convey from God and act upon His messages, so that I hold myself to what I command others." It has also been said: *al-risalat* (الرِّسالاتُ) is coordinated with the noble noun (*al-ism al-sharif*), meaning: "except a message from God and from His messages." Abu Hayyan said this and preferred it.

**﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger﴾** in the command to monotheism, because the context concerns it, **﴿then indeed for him is the Fire of Hell﴾**. The majority read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra, as an independent new sentence.

It has been read with a fatha on the hamza, because what follows the *fa'* of the apodosis is in the position of a new beginning, and the implied construction is *fa-jaza'uhu anna lahu nara jahannam* (فَجَزاؤُهُ أنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ), "so his recompense is that for him is the Fire of Hell," or *fa-hukmuhu anna lahu nara jahannam* (فَحُكْمُهُ أنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ), "so his judgement is that for him is the Fire of Hell."

*Khalidina fiha* (خالِدِينَ فِيها) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: "in the Fire" or "in Hell." The plural is according to the meaning of *man* (مَن), just as the singular in His words *fa-inna lahu* (فَإنَّ لَهُ) is according to its wording. His words **"forever" (abadan)** are an emphasis of the meaning of eternal abiding, meaning: abiding therein without end.

**﴿Until, when they see what they are promised﴾**, meaning the punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter.

The meaning is: they will not cease in their state of persistence in disbelief and enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, **until, when they see what they are promised**, **﴿they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾**, meaning: who is weaker in army, by which he would be given victory, and fewer in number: they or the believers?

**﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾**, meaning: I do not know whether the occurrence of the punishment you are promised is near. God, glorified be He, commanded him to say this to them in response to their saying to him: "When will this come about that you threaten us with?" 'Ata' said: He means that no one knows the Day of Resurrection except God alone. The meaning is that the knowledge of the time of the punishment is knowledge of the unseen, which no one knows except God.

The majority read *rabbi* (رَبِّي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. The two Harams (Makki and Madani) and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha.

In *man a'ada* (مَن أضْعَفُ), *man* is a relative pronoun, and *a'da'* (أضْعَفُ) is the predicate of an implied subject: meaning "he is weaker." The clause is the relative clause. It is also permissible for it to be interrogative, raised as a subject, with *a'da'* as its predicate, and the clause is in the position of an accusative filling the place of the two objects of *adri* (أدْرِي). His words *aqarib* (أقَرِيبٌ) are a fronted predicate, and *ma tu'adun* (ما تُوعَدُونَ) is a delayed subject.

**﴿Knower of the unseen﴾**: the majority read it in the nominative, as a substitute for *rabbi*, or an apposition to it, or the predicate of an implied subject, and the clause is a new sentence affirming what precedes it of lacking knowledge.

It has been read in the accusative as praise.

As-Sari read *'alima al-ghayb* (عَلِمَ الغَيْبَ) with a verbal form and the accusative of *al-ghayb*. The *fa'* in **﴿So He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾** indicates the sequence of non-disclosure upon His singular knowledge of the unseen, meaning: He does not inform anyone of the unseen, which is what is hidden from His servants.

Then He made an exception, saying: **﴿except whom He has approved of of the messengers﴾**, meaning: except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, or whom He has approved of among them, for disclosing to him some of His unseen, so that this would be a sign of his prophethood.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 72, verses 14–28 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: When Allah (exalted is He) praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and reserved it for Himself to the exclusion of His creation, this is evidence that no one knows the unseen besides Him. Then He made an exception for whomever He approves of among the Messengers, so He entrusts them with whatever of His unseen He wills, by way of revelation to them. He makes this a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. The astrologer (munajjim) and whoever resembles him, from those who cast pebbles, read palms, and divine by mud, are not among the Messengers whom He approves and then informs of whatever He wills of His unseen. Such a person is a disbeliever in Allah, a fabricator against Him through his conjecture, his guesswork, and his lies.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" refers to Jibril (Gabriel). This interpretation is remote.

It has also been said that the meaning of "Except whom He approves of among the Messengers" is that He informs him of some of His unseen, namely what relates to his mission, such as miracles, the rulings of obligations, the reward for deeds, and what He clarifies of the conditions of the Hereafter. It does not include unseen matters that do not relate to his mission, such as the time of the Hour and the like.

Al-Wahidi said: In this is evidence that whoever claims that the stars guide him to what will happen of events has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: In this is a refutation of miracles (karamat) of saints, because those who are attributed to them, even if they are approved saints, are not Messengers. Allah has specifically singled out the Messengers from among the approved ones with knowledge of the unseen. It is also a refutation of soothsaying (kihanah) and astrology (tanjim), because their practitioners are the furthest thing from being approved and the most deserving of wrath.

Al-Razi said: In my view, the verse contains no evidence for any of what they have said, since there is no general formula (sigha 'umum) in "His unseen." It is therefore restricted to one unseen matter, namely the time of the Resurrection, because it comes after His words: ﴿Is what you are promised near, or does my Lord set for it a distant term?﴾ (al-Jinn: 25).

If it is said: What then is the meaning of the exception in this case? We say: Perhaps when the Resurrection draws near He will make it manifest. And how could it not be so, when He said: ﴿On the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾ (al-Furqan: 25). Then the angels will know at that time the establishment of the Resurrection. Or the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: whomever He approves of among the Messengers, He places before him and behind him guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious jinn and humans.

What indicates that the intended meaning is not "He does not inform anyone of any of the unseen matters" is that it is established, in what approaches mass-transmission (mutawatir), that Shiqq and Satih were two soothsayers. They knew about the Prophet's ﷺ affair before his emergence, and they were famous for this knowledge among the Arabs, to the extent that Kisra (Khosrow) consulted them.

Thus it is established that Allah (exalted is He) may inform non-Messengers of some unseen matters. Also, the people of the religions (ahl al-milal) unanimously agree that the interpreter of dreams (mu'abbir al-ru'ya) reports future matters and is truthful in them. Also, Sultan Sanjar ibn Malik Shah transported a female soothsayer from Baghdad to Khurasan, asked her about future matters, and she informed him of them, and events happened in accordance with her words.

He said: People of verification (muhaqqiqun) in kalam and wisdom informed me that she reported unseen events in detail, and they occurred in accordance with her report.

Abu al-Barakat exaggerated in the book of ta'bir (interpretation) in describing her condition, and said: He investigated her condition for thirty years, and he verified that she used to report unseen matters with accurate correspondence.

Also, we witness this in people of true inspirations (ilhamat), and it is found among sorcerers as well. We also see astrological judgments matching, although they may differ. If we said that the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an, and the interpretation would be what we mentioned. End of his words.

I say: As for his statement that "there is no general formula in His unseen," it is false, because the annexation of a verbal noun (masdar) and a generic noun (ism jins) are among the formulas of generality, as the leading scholars of legal theory (usul) and others have stated.

As for his statement, "or the exception is disjunctive," it is a mere claim that the Qur'anic arrangement rejects.

As for his statement, "that Shiqq and Satih etc.," they lived in a time when the devils eavesdropped and passed what they heard to the soothsayers, so they mixed truth with falsehood, as established in the sound hadith.

In His saying ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ (al-Saffat: 10) and similar verses, and the matter of soothsaying has been explained in this Sharia, and that it was a path to some of the unseen through the devils' eavesdropping, until they were prevented from it by the Muhammadan mission.

They said: ﴿And we touched the sky, and found it filled with strong guards and flaming fires. And we used to sit in it on seats for listening, but whoever listens now finds a watching flame awaiting him﴾ (al-Jinn: 8–9). So the practice of soothsaying at the time it existed is specified by its own evidences, and it is among what this general statement is restricted by. Therefore, what he claims about the soothsaying's bearing on this verse is not a valid objection.

As for the story of the woman that he cited, it is a fable. Even if we grant the occurrence of some of the reports he narrated from her, it would be among what is in the hadith: "Among this community there are muhaddathun (those who are inspired), and among them is 'Umar." It would then be like a specification of the generality of this verse, not an implication of it. As for what he dared to say against Allah and His Book in the end of his statement, "if we said the Qur'an indicates the opposite of these observable matters, criticism would reach the Qur'an," it is said to him: This is not your first slip, nor your first fall. How many similar and analogous things does the vein of your philosophy throb with, and the devil has spurred you so that he has you stumbling in the investigations of your tafsir! How strange you are! Would what reached you of the report of this woman and the like necessitate that criticism reach the Qur'an? How well said was the statement of one of the men of letters of our era:

"When the fly wishes to cover the sun, it spreads its wing over it."

And I said, among verses:

"A wind's path, it blocked it with a wing, and set a lamp against the light of dawn."

If you say: Then it has been established by this Qur'anic evidence that Allah reveals to whichever of His Messengers He approves whatever He wills of His unseen. Is it permissible for the Messenger to whom Allah revealed whatever He willed of His unseen to inform some of his community of it? I say: Yes, and there is no prohibition against that.

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of this what is not hidden from one knowledgeable in the pure Sunnah. Among that is what is sound: that he stood at a station (maqam) in which he informed of what would happen until the Day of Resurrection, and he left nothing that relates to trials (fitan) and the like unmentioned. Whoever memorized it memorized it, and whoever forgot it forgot it.

Likewise, what is established that Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman had been informed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the trials that would occur after him, to the extent that the senior Companions asked him about that and returned to him.

It is established in the Sahih and elsewhere that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked him about the trial that surges like the surging of the sea. He said: "Between you and it there is a door."
